non_verbatim_nodes.text: 20th meeting of the Special Committee on the COVID-19 Pandemic; reminder that in-person members shouldn't also be on video conference, and video participants must use the language-matched audio channel
Blair tables the 2019 annual report on the RCMP's use of law-enforcement justification provisions (Criminal Code ss. 25), covering the nature of investigations where they were used
Sajjan tables the 2018-19 progress report on Canada's national action plan implementing UN Security Council resolutions on women, peace and security
**Petitions presented** (chair reminds members to be concise)

May — an e-petition on pollinator decline from neonicotinoid pesticides (EU has already acted), calling for a precautionary ban; a second petition on southern resident killer whales, calling for boat-free safety zones, tourism restrictions, and stronger enforcement

Genuis — support for Bill S-204 against forced organ harvesting/trafficking abroad, noting a decade of cross-party bills on the issue and suggesting government could bring forward its own bill to speed things up

Cannings — support for Motion M-1, a "green new deal," calling for bold climate action alongside socio-economic/racial equity, ending fossil-fuel subsidies, closing offshore tax havens, and green-transition jobs

Johns — e-petition (5,183 signatures) for a guaranteed livable basic income, timed near the anniversary of the National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls, which made a similar call

Manly — halt Coastal GasLink construction on Wet'suwet'en territory, order the RCMP to stand down its exclusion zone, hold nation-to-nation talks (noted as already happening, which he commends), and prioritize the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples
Lamoureux — on behalf of Winnipeg North constituents, asks Canada/MPs to be attentive to Guyana's contested March presidential election and to advocate for democracy there
**Member statements** (~14 MPs, mostly local COVID-response tributes)
Lefebvre — thanks Sudbury's workers/innovators (ProStitch/King Sportswear masks, Crosscut hand sanitizer, SNOLAB ventilator work, Vale's $1M seed capital)
Dalton — describes Pitt Meadows' history/geography and a distanced community "parade" cheering essential workers
Kelloway — highlights individual Cape Breton–Canso community-support acts (iPad delivery to seniors, meal delivery, youth outreach, flower deliveries)
Brébeuf (BQ) — calls for a commission of inquiry into police brutality against Indigenous people (echoing Romeo Saganash), citing unimplemented Viens Commission and MMIWG recommendations
MacKinnon — congratulates Gatineau-area high school graduates missing traditional ceremonies
Morantz — highlights the Bruce Oake Recovery Centre construction, built in memory of an overdose death, amid Canada's addictions crisis
Jowhari — thanks Richmond Hill charities/care centres for pandemic donations and services
Lalonde — highlights Orléans-area grade-12 graduates and community gestures honoring them
Vis — highlights rural/Indigenous internet-access gaps worsened by remote work/school, calls for a federal connectivity action plan
McLeod — celebrates Canada's first Equator Prize (UN) for the Thaidene Nëné Indigenous-led protected area, thanks past environment minister for a $7.9M commitment
xi. Falk — criticizes only 4 hours allotted to scrutinize $87B in spending as inadequate parliamentary oversight
xii. Godin — tribute to seniors, students, and essential workers in Portneuf–Jacques-Cartier
xiii. Gazan — honors Justice 4 Black Lives Winnipeg, condemns police brutality and systemic racism, links Indigenous and Black liberation
xiv. DeBellefeuille (BQ) — accuses the PM of "locking down" Parliament to avoid accountability, withholding an economic update and refusing a first ministers' meeting on health transfers
xv. Uppal — thanks Edmonton Mill Woods' multicultural/faith organizations for meal and grocery delivery to seniors, families, and truckers
xvi. Fonseca — marks Portugal Day/Portuguese Heritage Month, thanks the ~500,000-strong Luso-Canadian community for resilience during the pandemic
accuses the PM of avoiding accountability (no budget, no economic update, limiting House sittings); asks whether the AG will get additional funding
cites the AG's own statement that she can now complete only ~14 performance audits/year versus ~27 a decade ago, despite government spending nearly doubling

cites interim AG John Wiersema's past statement that earlier administrative efficiencies (not funding cuts) were the office's own choice and didn't affect its mandate — implying today's shortfall is different and government-caused
Trudeau repeatedly redirects to the day's disability/CERB/wage-subsidy bill and a proposed debate/vote, without ever answering "yes or no"

Trudeau/Guilbeault repeat that the government added the equivalent of 38 new full-time staff to the AG's office in 2018-19, contrasted with 60 positions cut under the prior Harper government (a comparison Scheer calls "revisionist history," countering that 2015 was the only election Trudeau won more votes than the Conservatives)
congratulates the new Auditor General, then repeats the funding question directly; Guilbeault initially discusses wanting to "work with her" rather than answering
disputes the "60 positions cut" framing, saying committee transcripts show the AG's office chose to reduce its own budget, not that the Conservatives cut it

notes the AG has already cut/stopped performance audits for lack of funds, and that the House finance committee (with Liberal backbench support) unanimously passed a motion to fully fund her office the day before
Guilbeault switches briefly to French "in case it's clearer," repeats the 38-staff figure and a general "if she identifies a need, we'll work with her" pledge, never committing to the specific ask
Kelly later invokes Standing Orders to suggest the PM "misled the House," citing public-accounts-committee transcripts, but the Acting Chair rules this is turning into debate and moves on
frames the bill as "chocolate pudding containing cod liver oil" — supports the disability-aid part but not the rest — and explains a bill can procedurally be divided and voted on in parts

repeatedly asks Trudeau to confirm he'll split it so the disability portion passes immediately; Trudeau's "all or some of the measures" answer is read by Blanchet as tacit confirmation, but Trudeau never explicitly confirms a split

separately criticizes the government's proposed CERB changes as overly coercive, arguing the wage subsidy's lack of a work incentive already undermined that program, and insists the bill doesn't need "eight months," just a proper committee process with amendments — contrasting this with what he calls "rubber-stamping"
references the October 2019 election producing a minority government as grounds the government shouldn't act like it holds a majority
Trudeau cites providing the bill text to opposition four days early and "hours" of amendment discussions as evidence of good-faith process, given pandemic urgency

presses repeatedly (5 times) for a direct yes/no on extending CERB for families with no work to return to; cites a specific constituent ("Don from Burnaby," an arts worker) fearing CERB's end-of-month expiry; Trudeau avoids a direct answer each time, citing "ongoing discussions" and redirecting to the day's three proposed measures (disability support, wage-subsidy expansion, CERB flexibility)

flags that the disability-support payment, based on the disability tax credit, will reach only ~40% of Canadians with disabilities, excluding many veterans and CPP/disability-payment recipients — often the poorest; Trudeau claims the measure covers "100% of Canadians who receive the disability tax credit" without addressing the excluded 60%, and accuses the NDP of blocking debate/passage entirely by not allowing a vote

counters that a tax-credit approach is fundamentally the wrong mechanism, and states the NDP's conditions for support: extend CERB, remove penalties on those in need, and help all disabled Canadians — Trudeau again avoids a direct commitment, framing the ask as "playing political games"

covers three elements: a one-time $600 disability-support payment (reaching an estimated 1.25 million people via the disability tax credit), CERB eligibility flexibility (four-week windows shortened to two weeks), and expanded wage-subsidy access for more businesses

raises a travel-agency owner with no work to return to, hitting the CERB "wall" in four weeks; separately criticizes proposed penalty provisions as "talking about jailing people" and invokes a 51-year-old bartender with no job to return to, asking a direct yes/no on CERB's July continuation; Qualtrough and Fortier each answer with general "we'll continue to support Canadians" language, no commitment
Blanchette-Joncas: Quebec tourism recovery outlook is bleak; asks if CERB will extend beyond 16 weeks for tourism workers; Qualtrough (tired, switching to English) promises "news soon" without a date

notes seasonal industries don't qualify for the wage subsidy under current criteria, asks for CERB to include an employment incentive instead of ending outright; Qualtrough repeats the "don't disincentivize work" framing without committing

Trudel: cites a closed Longueuil café and a restaurant owner uncertain of reopening capacity/hours, asks directly "will CERB be extended on July 5?"; Qualtrough answers only "we will be there for Canadian workers in July," no specifics; Joly separately points to CED regional funding for restaurants

Bragdon: separately raises a New Brunswick potato farmer sitting on unsold surplus crop a month after a $50M food-surplus purchase program was announced, with no funds yet delivered; Mendicino cites "hundreds of millions" for farmers generally and migrant-worker support, without addressing the delay
repeatedly presses Morneau for an economic update by end of June, noting most provinces are doing so; Morneau defers, citing the importance of "transparency" without committing to a date
notes the Parliamentary Budget Officer is independently calling for an update; Morneau repeats a "daily information" framing instead of a formal update
accuses the government of ignoring experts/opposition/provinces when their advice is inconvenient ("terrible twos" analogy), while listening to scientists when convenient

separately raises that a month-old promise to expand CEBA eligibility to self-employed/dividend-paying businesses still isn't implemented — officials confirmed on a June 2 technical call that information wouldn't be available for "several weeks" more; Fortier (Minister of Middle Class Prosperity) cites expanded eligibility to businesses with payrolls under $20,000 and says financial institutions are adapting, without a fix date

cites Global News reporting on Canada's struggle to secure reliable PPE: 10 million substandard N95 masks that couldn't be used, masks returned to suppliers, moldy COVID-test swabs received, empty planes that should have carried PPE, and under 5% of a total glove order received
Bains cites over 700 Canadian companies mobilized to retool/rescale for domestic PPE production as part of a made-in-Canada initiative

Anand disputes some specifics as "tainted with inaccuracies" — says Air Canada reimbursed the government for an empty-cargo flight, the government won't pay for unused masks, and over half of received face shields were domestically produced

contrasts strict public-health enforcement on ordinary Canadians (fines for park visits, restaurant patio fines, wedding restrictions, Skype goodbyes to dying relatives) against the PM's son attending a large gathering without distancing; Hajdu responds by pivoting to anti-racism solidarity and deferring to local public-health guidance, not addressing the comparison directly
cites Morneau's March 25 promise of help "within hours, possibly days" for the energy sector; notes 77 days later, no energy company has received EDC, BDC, or LEEFF financing

cites the Canadian Association of Petroleum Producers (frustration with delay) and Saskatchewan's energy minister ("gaping hole" in support); notes eligibility criteria for EDC/BDC weren't even finalized 54 days after the April 17 announcement, confirmed by BDC/EDC officials at finance committee the day prior
mocks a BDC website feature letting companies "sign up for email updates" as inadequate relief after 77 days

O'Regan cites support from the Business Council of Alberta and Alberta's finance minister for the LEEFF program, frames the sector as facing dual crises (COVID plus a Saudi-Russia price war), and reiterates liquidity measures for small/medium players (85% of sector jobs) and larger players via LEEFF, without a specific date for disbursement

raises constituents in business nearly 30 years, with hundreds of HST returns filed, still unable to access CEBA because they use personal rather than business chequing accounts; Joly points to Minister Ng's ongoing work and regional development agencies as a funding backstop, without a specific fix date
Quebec estimates ~$3B in additional COVID health costs; federal transfer is ~$115M, under 4% of that; presses whether the government recognizes this as insufficient
Hajdu cites an initial $500M transfer package plus ongoing $40B in existing transfers, without directly addressing the gap or committing to more

Ste-Marie reframes the issue as "needs," not "squabbling," cites federal health-transfer disinvestment as the root cause, and presses for a commitment to a first ministers' meeting with Quebec/provinces on funding by September at the latest, ahead of a possible second wave; no direct commitment given

confirms via La Presse reporting that ~500 soldiers remain in Quebec long-term care homes at Quebec's request; Blair confirms the request and ongoing conversation with Quebec's counterpart minister, noting other forms of assistance (e.g., Canadian Red Cross) could supplement

presses for a firm extension given the mission's Friday end date and the urgency of training replacement staff; Blair commits Canadian Armed Forces support through mid-September, working with Quebec and the Red Cross
Brunelle-Duceppe notes Quebec funds 23% of the military's budget and has lost 5,000+ residents (90% in care homes), framing continued support as owed, not negotiated
thanks the government for progress on a consular case (André Gauthier) before pivoting to economic asks

criticizes inflexible program design favoring Montreal SMEs over regional needs; Joly cites $71M in additional Quebec regional funding (announced that morning on Radio-Canada) and offers to work with him via the CFDC in his region — dismissed by Martel as a "canned speech"

cites a Université de Trois-Rivières survey ranking Saguenay–Lac-Saint-Jean as the most economically affected region, listing forestry, aluminum, GNL Québec, tourism, the Port of Saguenay, Davie Canada, a military base, and a tax centre as regional assets needing support

separately raises sustainable forestry's role in climate strategy and asks who will defend forestry workers amid existing sector problems plus COVID; Joly defers to working with the Minister of Natural Resources
flags the draft bill as "unacceptable" to her caucus, previewing that her questions target its troublesome sections

notes the $600 one-time disability payment, structured via the disability tax credit, will reach only ~40% of disabled Canadians (a figure she credits to Singh raising it in Question Period); asks what other measures are under consideration for the rest

Qualtrough lists complementary measures — CERB access for precariously employed disabled people, a $750/month student top-up, CCB payments for families with disabled children, the GST credit, and provincial-disability-support letters — without directly committing to closing the coverage gap

challenges a proposed "reasonableness" test (bill's proposed s. 12.1) that could subject people refusing work to jail time/fines, calling it subjective and pointing to a Hamilton medical officer's report of a COVID spike among young transit commuters as evidence "reasonable" is not a simple bar

calls the approach punitive rather than incentivizing, suggests the government has been unduly swayed by Conservative "fraud" rhetoric, and proposes a sliding-scale CERB/wage-subsidy transition instead of penalties

Qualtrough frames "reasonableness" as capturing individual circumstances (e.g., immunocompromised workers unable to take transit), says the measure targets intentional/criminal fraud (e.g., targeting seniors) flagged by MPs themselves, not honest mistakes, but (citing parliamentary privilege) declines to discuss the not-yet-introduced bill's specific text further
invokes George Floyd's death and Viola Desmond's legacy to frame anti-Black racism as institutionalized in Canada too, and links it to anti-Asian sentiment during the pandemic
cites StatCan data on Black youth being pushed into the justice system, asks what's being done for Black youth specifically

Chagger cites 2016 census figures (1.2M Black Canadians, over a quarter under 15), a youth-created national youth policy, a 56-project Black-Canadian-youth support program (leadership, civic engagement, cultural promotion), and pandemic-specific youth/student employment measures, with outreach to community organizations serving Black youth
notes many child-care providers face reduced capacity under COVID and argues universal, publicly funded child care is needed to restart the economy; asks for legislated federal funding
Hussen cites 40,000 spaces created since 2015 and a commitment to 250,000 more before/after-school spaces

Mathyssen counters this isn't universal child care, notes women bore most pandemic job losses and added care burden, and that 26 years of Liberal promises on national child care remain unfulfilled; separately challenges new legislation she frames as threatening jail time/fines for parents who can't find child care

Hussen reiterates the $7.5B/11-year investment commitment and a planned "early learning and child care secretariat," without addressing the universality critique or the penalty-provision question directly

raises pregnant/postpartum women being denied EI benefits or told to return to work despite gaps in coverage; Qualtrough says she's "working hard" on a fix "very soon," referencing a prior fix for fish harvesters as precedent, without details

presses (repeated 5 times across the exchange) on whether a Gender-Based Analysis Plus (GBA+) was conducted on COVID relief programs before rollout, given the PM's stated commitment to rigorous GBA+ for all legislation; Qualtrough never confirms or denies one was conducted, repeating that women's needs were "taken into account from the beginning" and citing benefits like the GST credit and CCB payment reaching women

Sahota accuses the minister of dodging responsibility; Qualtrough claims to "take responsibility" while citing statistics on women helped, without answering the GBA+ question even in her final (5-second) answer

during National Blood Donor Week, argues behavior-based screening (used in 17+ other countries) is scientifically superior to the current identity-based deferral, and notes the Liberals promised to end the ban in two election campaigns; Duclos (Treasury Board President, answering for Health) offers general anti-discrimination sentiment without lifting the ban

notes he's personally recruiting allies to donate blood in place of excluded gay men, and stresses urgent need for convalescent plasma donations for COVID research specifically, rejected under the current ban; Duclos again cites "progress" without action

recalls tabling a motion six years earlier (five health ministers ago) calling for the ban's end, with preconditions supposedly meant to be resolved before COVID hit; asks for unanimous consent to fast-track his new motion M-41 given apparent cross-party support; Duclos responds with general anti-discrimination language, no commitment to M-41 or a ban repeal date
**Parole Board video access for victims (Carrie, CPC)**

recalls an April 29 exchange where Minister Blair acknowledged a constituent (Lisa Freeman) couldn't join her father's murderer's parole hearing, and promised victims could join by phone/video going forward; asks how many hearings have used the digital format for victims since
Mendicino repeatedly says the number will be "provided in due course" without giving it across multiple follow-ups

cites the Parole Board's own website distinguishing that staff/inmates get video conference while victims are explicitly limited to telephone participation; presses why the discrepancy exists, and later accuses the government of telling Canadians something untrue about equal access
Mendicino defends the process as "fair" and citing "technology and innovations introduced by the Board," without directly resolving the phone-vs-video discrepancy or providing hearing counts

cites the May 1 order-in-council banning 1,500 firearms, notes reports of further additions including common hunting rifles/shotguns, and frames hunters/sport shooters/dealers as among the most vetted members of society
Mendicino defends the policy as targeting guns whose "one objective is to kill people," pledging continued community-safety measures

Bragdon proposes redirecting the estimated ~$250M buyback cost to agricultural support instead; Mendicino reiterates the public-safety rationale and separately cites "hundreds of millions" already committed to farmers, without addressing the buyback-reallocation proposal directly

describes tourism in his riding as "burned to the ground" after a promising pre-pandemic outlook, with over half of local tourism businesses facing imminent insolvency, many too small/seasonal to qualify for existing programs; asks for direct, timely support beyond ad-campaign funding

Joly cites the extended wage subsidy (to end of August), CEBA loans, commercial rent relief, and a regional-development-agency backstop (Western Economic Diversification in his riding), inviting him to bring specific business cases to her

flags that the wine industry's excise-tax exemption (key to the sector's growth) may soon be ruled non-compliant with trade agreements, and that industry has proposed a trade-legal replacement (the wine growers' value-added program) that Morneau has known about "for months"; Morneau promises only to "come back... with an update," no commitment given

notes medical-provider costs rising faster than Veterans Affairs' rate-scale adjustments (up to a year lag), with no retroactive reimbursement allowed; MacAulay cites a general $10B investment in veterans' supports (pension for life, PTSD/chronic-pain centres of excellence) without addressing the retroactivity gap

notes constituents find seniors' support inadequate amid inflation from pandemic spending, and cites an opposition proposal for a one-time tax-free RRSP/RRIF withdrawal the government hasn't acted on; Schulte cites a 25% reduction in 2020 minimum RRIF withdrawals plus direct financial support, without addressing the specific RRSP/RRIF withdrawal proposal

presses for the repatriation of André Gauthier, stranded in the UAE without a passport awaiting civil-lawsuit resolution; Garneau confirms the file is "active" via consular services, no timeline given

notes citizens who fell ill before March 15 are denied both CERB (didn't lose jobs due to COVID) and regular EI (unable to work), with some also facing delayed surgeries; Qualtrough cites a commitment to extend EI sickness benefits from 15 to 26 weeks as addressing this, in progress

cites Hong Kong's ~9,000 arrests in the past year (proportionally equivalent to 42,000 in Canada) amid Beijing's new national-security law, and asks whether Canada has begun preparing a Magnitsky-sanctions list; Garneau cites "deep concern" among Canada and allies and defends Hong Kong's "one country, two systems" autonomy, without confirming any sanctions preparation

notes China's embassy has "deplored, rejected and condemned" Canada's stated concerns, and presses on what conditions would trigger sanctions if incarcerations continue; Garneau calls for continued "peaceful and meaningful dialogue," no conditions specified

in a final 22-second exchange, cites China's COVID-19 statements and two detained Canadians, asking when Canada will call for a stronger, independent international investigation into COVID-19's origin; Garneau calls generally for global transparency and cooperation, without endorsing a specific investigative mechanism
asks why a 14-day quarantine can't be lifted via antibody test for exposed individuals; Hajdu notes testing strategy is a provincial/territorial responsibility and timing-sensitive

cites a specific antibody test (90% accurate, already sold to the US and other countries via a constituent connection through fellow MP Colin Carrie) not yet approved with a Canadian DIN number; Hajdu distinguishes market-access questions from Health Canada's rigor requirements and asks for the company's name to follow up

presses on turnaround time once a company/test is identified; Hajdu cites an expedited process "as little as five to seven days" depending on accuracy/vendor data — which Gallant then contrasts with cases reportedly taking 30-90+ days, without Hajdu reconciling the discrepancy directly
asks whether international data could speed determinations; Hajdu reiterates Health Canada's own accuracy/safety standards

asks whether officials have set a daily antibody-testing target for an initial survey; Hajdu references the government-funded immunity task force (a group of scientists) without giving a numeric target
asks for the task force members' names; Hajdu commits to forwarding them to her office "within the next two days," which Gallant notes she'll hold them to

closes by contrasting the government's urgency for a vaccine versus antibody testing; Hajdu "rejects the premise," calling the suggestion disingenuous and citing the PM's consistent engagement since the pandemic's start
per Standing Orders (April 20/May 26), the House is recalled; committee adjourns as the full House prepares to sit at 2:30 p.m.

presses Trudeau to fund the Auditor General fully so she can conduct audits amid rising government spending

cites difficulty projecting amid a "dynamic" situation; commits only to continued daily disclosure of investments, not a formal update

presses for a firm extension commitment; Blair commits to support through mid-September while professional replacements are trained, working with the Red Cross

presses for support to Saguenay–Lac-Saint-Jean's forestry, aluminum, tourism and port sectors; Joly cites $71M in new regional funding and ongoing conversations, without addressing the region's specific asks directly

presses whether other measures will reach the ~60% of disabled Canadians excluded by the tax-credit-based $600 payment; Qualtrough lists complementary measures (CERB, student top-up, CCB, GST credit) without a direct commitment to close the gap

challenges a subjective "reasonableness" test in the bill that could jail CERB recipients for refusing work; Qualtrough frames it as accounting for individual circumstances (e.g., immunocompromised workers), aimed at intentional fraud, not honest mistakes

asks what's being done for Black youth amid the George Floyd killing and Statistics Canada data on disparities; Chagger cites a youth policy and a 56-project Black-youth support program, plus pandemic-specific measures

presses for legislated universal child care, noting women bore the pandemic's job losses and added care burden; Hussen cites 40,000 spaces created since 2015 and a $7.5B/11-year commitment for 250,000 more, without addressing universality

presses repeatedly (5+ times) on why no gender-based analysis was done before rollout, leaving pregnant/postpartum women without EI access; Qualtrough repeats that women's needs were "taken into account," without answering whether a GBA+ was actually conducted

during National Blood Donor Week, presses to lift the ban (twice promised in past campaigns), noting 17+ countries use behavior-based screening instead; Duclos cites "progress" and ongoing work without lifting the ban or supporting Garrison's motion M-41

presses repeatedly on why crime victims can only join parole hearings by phone while inmates/staff get video conference, despite an April 29 promise of equal access; Mendicino repeatedly says victims "are able to participate" without confirming video access or hearing counts

challenges the May 1 ban on 1,500 firearms as targeting law-abiding hunters/sport shooters, and suggests redirecting the ~$250M buyback budget to agriculture instead; Mendicino defends the ban as targeting guns "meant to kill people" and cites separate farm funding

seasonal tourism businesses ineligible for existing programs need direct support (Joly points to regional development agency backstops); wine industry needs a replacement for an excise-tax exemption likely to be ruled trade-non-compliant (Morneau promises to "come back" with an update)
veterans face up to a year's wait for medical-cost rate adjustments with no retroactive reimbursement; MacAulay cites $10B invested in veterans' supports generally, without addressing retroactivity
seniors' RRIF minimum withdrawals reduced 25% for 2020 as inflation/market volatility concerns are raised; Schulte cites this plus direct financial support
presses for repatriation of a Canadian (André Gauthier) stranded in the UAE without a passport; Garneau says the file remains active, no timeline given

presses for Magnitsky-style sanctions over Hong Kong's national security law and detained Canadians, and for an independent COVID-origin investigation; Garneau reiterates "deep concern" and calls for dialogue, without committing to sanctions

non_verbatim_nodes.text: sixth meeting of the House of Commons Special Committee on the COVID-19 pandemic, held by videoconference; reminders to use language-matched channels, speak through the chair, speak slowly for interpreters, and use headsets (explicitly recommended for both fellow members and interpreters, given feedback/squeaking issues)
none today; petitions period capped at 15 minutes, chair reminds members petitions must be a "concise précis," not a speech (specifically redirecting Mr. Vis mid-petition)

McPherson (NDP) — on behalf of the Canadian Perinatal Mental Health Collaborative, timed to World Maternal Mental Health Day: cites 20% of women/10% of men affected by perinatal mood/anxiety disorders, an $11B annual economic cost, and that the UK/Australia/parts of the US already have strategies Canada lacks; calls for a national strategy with universal screening and timely treatment access

Reid (CPC) — Cystic Fibrosis Awareness Month; cites CF as the top disease-killer of young Canadians; asks that Patented Medicine Prices Review Board regulatory changes be rescinded, since they'd restrict access to CF/other medications, especially Trikafta (effective for ~90% of CF sufferers); asks government to negotiate a joint provincial gene-modulator pricing strategy

May (GP) — pre-dates the pandemic; cites nearly 5 million Canadians lacking a family doctor, especially acute in rural communities like her own (Sidney, BC); calls for collaborative federal-provincial-territorial action

Vis (CPC) — constituents oppose firearms legislation/regulation as "undemocratic"; calls to stop targeting licensed, RCMP-vetted owners, cancel confiscation plans, redirect funding to anti-gang/at-risk-youth programs, and resource CBSA to intercept illegal gun smuggling; notes "military-style assault rifle" is an undefined political term in Canadian law

Johns (NDP) — e-petition (1,198 signers, mostly Nova Scotia) opposing Nova Scotia's invitation to multinational open-net salmon farming; cites environmental-degradation precedent from BC/Newfoundland/Norway/Vietnam, risks to wild Atlantic salmon and lobster/other fisheries, and limited job creation; calls to uphold Bill C-68/species-at-risk law, ban expansion, phase out existing open-net farms, and invest in closed-containment aquaculture

Manly (GP) — Nanaimo–Ladysmith constituents call to halt Coastal GasLink construction on Wet'suwet'en territory, order the RCMP to stand down its exclusion zone, hold nation-to-nation talks (noted as already underway), and prioritize UNDRIP implementation
Ratansi (Lib.) — Don Valley East constituents ask that no federal financial assistance go to Canadian or foreign airlines until full refunds are issued for COVID-cancelled flights

opens by citing a media report that federal workers were told to ignore "obvious signs of fraud" when processing benefit applications, and asks Trudeau to confirm ~200,000 applications were flagged as potentially fraudulent
Trudeau's initial answer emphasizes speed of CERB/wage-subsidy rollout and "we recognize there will be challenges... we will work through those"
Albas repeats the confirmation request on the 200,000-flagged-applications figure specifically; Trudeau again pivots to "helping as many people as possible" and "retroactive action if necessary"

Albas asks (citing the memo's origin with a deputy minister) whether the minister's office or PM signed off on it; Trudeau's answer notes "other parties might have made a different choice" but doesn't confirm or deny sign-off

Albas repeats the same yes/no question three more times across the exchange, explicitly naming it as an accountability test ("show some accountability," "leave the cottage talk for the cottage"); Trudeau never answers directly, each time returning to the "help first, clean up after" framing and implying opposition parties would have been slower

Albas asks whether the PM will commit to investigating every individual fraud case, or "write them off" as the story suggested; Trudeau responds with a broader statement about Canadians' job/paycheque losses and the need to support them, not addressing investigation specifically

Albas clarifies the Conservatives supported the enabling legislation and are specifically asking about fraud enforcement per the program's attestation requirement; asks Trudeau to confirm audits will happen; Trudeau confirms only in general terms that "we will do that" (go after fraudulent cases) as part of cleanup, with no specifics on scope or timeline
asks the Minister of National Revenue directly whether CRA sent a memo instructing employees to send CERB payments even where fraud was detected, per a national media report that day
Lebouthillier's first answer discusses "difficult times" and government support generally, then is interrupted before finishing a sentence about "nearly seven million" CERB applicants
Rayes repeats the direct yes/no question a second time; Lebouthillier finishes her earlier sentence (7.8 million Canadians applied) without answering
on the third repetition, explicitly phrased as "yes or no," Lebouthillier answers "no"

Rayes pivots to CERB repayment mechanics: the government website says a returning worker must repay CERB, but doesn't specify whether it's $500 per week worked or the full $2,000/month; asks Trudeau (redirected to ministers) for a direct number
Qualtrough's first answer: Service Canada will work with anyone transitioning off CERB to avoid overpayment or "undue hardship," without a number

Rayes notes this uncertainty has persisted "seven weeks" since program launch and both workers and companies need the number to plan; repeats the question a third time; Qualtrough answers only that it "depends on individual circumstances," reiterating outreach efforts, still no number

Rayes, with 35 seconds left, pivots to ask whether an employee can refuse to return to work (and keep collecting CERB) if the employer has met hygiene/safety conditions; Qualtrough cites existing federal/provincial work-refusal processes and reiterates CERB is meant for those not working specifically due to COVID, without resolving the underlying ambiguity for employers

opens sarcastically welcoming the Large Employer Emergency Financing Facility's anti-tax-evasion condition ("Excellent!") before noting it targets only "abusive" evasion/avoidance (i.e., fraud), not the legal use of tax havens by profitable companies; calls those companies "profiteers" and asks why the PM continues to "support" them
Trudeau responds with a general "no tolerance for tax evasion/avoidance" line and pivots to worker-support measures as the immediate priority

Ste-Marie distinguishes evasion (illegal) from avoidance (legal use of tax havens by "the five big Bay Street banks" and multinationals), asks whether the PM will move to outlaw what he calls "immoral" but legal practices; Trudeau says applying for the facility requires having "paid your fair share," with tax structures "carefully assessed" case by case before loans are issued

gives a concrete example — a bank relocating its most profitable Canadian activities to a subsidiary in the Bahamas or Barbados — and asks whether that still counts as "fair share"; Trudeau says applications are assessed case-by-case, notes big banks aren't expected to need the facility, and commits to requiring transparency about "how the money is being managed, including internationally," without directly answering the bank example

changes subject to credit-card interchange fees: notes contactless/online payment growth benefits Visa/Mastercard, whose fees are "almost 10 times higher than in Europe and Australia" and cost merchants heavily; asks Trudeau to cap fees at 0.3% as those jurisdictions did
Trudeau's answer discusses "reducing costs for consumers" and working with banks/financial industry generally, without addressing the merchant-fee/interchange-cap request

Ste-Marie clarifies the question isn't about consumers but merchants specifically (2.5-3% per-transaction fees eating into margins); repeats the 0.3% cap request; Trudeau says "some things we can look at over the longer term," no commitment
**Savard-Tremblay's (BQ) push for an executive-compensation cap (long preamble)**

frames the crisis as an opportunity for a "transition," arguing what's merely unjust in normal times becomes "scandalous" in crisis, and that it's legitimate for the state to attach conditions when companies request aid

cites Quebec precedent: after the Bombardier controversy, three of four National Assembly parties supported compensation limits on state-aided companies, a position also shared by Quebec civil-society groups and even implemented in periods of crisis in the (explicitly non-socialist) United States

cites a Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives report (published Jan. 2): the 100 highest-paid CEOs earned 227x the average worker in 2018; average worker pay rose 2.6% (2017-18, against 2.3% inflation — essentially flat in real terms) versus an 18% CEO pay increase, "even in cases where companies suffered losses" — all pre-dating the current crisis, which he suggests has since widened the gap into an "abyss"

asks directly whether the government will cap executive compensation so executives don't uniquely profit from crisis support, demanding "a clear answer," half-jokingly threatening to "demand a new version of the Clarity Act" if not

Morneau confirms the government's approach covers small/medium and large companies as a "bridge" to protect jobs and the economy via the Large Employer Emergency Financing Facility; confirms conditions were built in "from the outset," specifically citing executive-compensation limits as "very important," alongside prohibiting use of funds for dividends or share buybacks and reviewing companies' tax situations (including tax-evasion checks); promises "more details in the coming days" but gives no specific compensation ceiling number

criticizes the government's approach as "complicated" versus a universal direct payment, citing a specific case: a single parent of four school-age children who lost spousal/child support due to COVID, pays tax on that spousal income, but is CERB-ineligible; notes the Minister of Employment has acknowledged the gap for three weeks without action; asks Trudeau to personally intervene

Trudeau's response claims the government "moved in the most rapid and simplest possible way" reaching "millions upon millions" via CERB, concedes gaps are inevitable when moving quickly, and says they're "working diligently" to fill them, without addressing this specific case

Kwan repeats that three weeks of "looking into it" hasn't produced action, and that spousal/child support recipients specifically remain unsupported; Trudeau cites the increased Canada Child Benefit and "over seven million Canadians" with CERB access as partial mitigations, still not addressing spousal-support income specifically

describes the lack of a national homelessness standard during COVID: no bathroom access for basic hygiene, inability to social-distance in crowded SROs/shelters, particularly acute in her Downtown Eastside riding; notes BC's short-term hotel-housing initiative and asks for federal matching funds toward permanent post-COVID housing solutions and a "right to adequate housing"

Trudeau says the federal government sent "hundreds of millions of dollars" to shelters almost immediately for facility expansion, points to the National Housing Strategy's commitment to cut chronic homelessness, and says "there's always more to do"

Kwan calls the funding "deficient" and the 50%-chronic-homelessness-reduction-over-a-decade goal inadequate, calls it an "empty promise," and asks whether the government will guarantee a housing right and match provincial funding; Trudeau defends the 50% goal as "ambitious," unmatched by prior governments, and says the government is "well on track," while conceding "more to do"

Kwan notes it was federal Liberals who eliminated the national affordable-housing program in 1993, framing today's crisis as a direct consequence; cites Vancouver East having the third-largest urban Indigenous population in Canada yet receiving under 2% of pandemic urban-Indigenous-housing funding despite Indigenous overrepresentation among the homeless, and asks why; Trudeau acknowledges "more to do" for urban Indigenous people, cites work through the Ministers of Indigenous Services and Crown-Indigenous Relations, without addressing the 2%-funding-share figure specifically

cites the CERB rule that earning over $1,000 in a reporting period requires repaying the entire $2,000 benefit, describing it as a "classic Liberal catch-22" for part-time/casual workers who might unknowingly exceed the threshold "by a couple of dollars"; asks whether full repayment is really required in that case; Qualtrough notes the $1,000 allowance was itself a relaxation from an original zero-earnings rule, and that Service Canada is proactively reaching out to prevent "undue hardship," without addressing whether the cliff-edge design itself will change
Service Canada and administrative delays (Bergen, CPC)

cites a specific constituent whose documents, including a doctor's note, were mailed March 12 and are now — roughly two months later — being reported as never opened, requiring resubmission; asks whether unopened mail is a widespread Service Canada problem and how it's being addressed

Hussen cites unprecedented volumes, redeployment of "thousands of staff" to phone-based front-line service, and pandemic-driven office closures for safety; says he's not personally aware unopened mail is widespread and offers to look into the specific case directly with Bergen
asks why the Iver Johnson single-shot rifle — described as a farm gun "passed down from generation to generation" — was banned, and what public-safety purpose banning it serves

Blair explains the government worked with the Canadian firearms program, law enforcement, and firearms verification specialists to identify nine rifle makes/models/variants whose "earliest provenance" traces to military combat design

Bergen challenges whether front-line officers were actually consulted, saying front-line concerns center on gangs/drug dealers/smuggled illegal weapons, not registered farm rifles used for hunting; asks for the evidence behind targeting "law-abiding Canadians"

Blair cites specific police-association statements: the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police calling military assault rifles designed "for the sole purpose of killing people in large numbers" and urging a ban (with law-enforcement/military exceptions); Ontario police leaders' statement that such weapons "have no place in our communities"

Bergen invokes the costly, ineffective long-gun registry as historical precedent for skepticism, and asks directly whether the minister is calling the Iver Johnson an "assault rifle"; Blair clarifies the criterion is design intent (for soldiers to kill other soldiers), not the specific term "assault rifle," and reiterates that any Canadian gun death is "one too many"

cites Wanstalls, a downtown Maple Ridge firearms retailer employing 8 people and serving "thousands" of law-abiding local gun owners, now holding tens of thousands of dollars in unsellable banned inventory; asks what recourse the owners (Craig and Matt) have; Blair reiterates that hunting/sport-shooting firearms remain fully legal and available, and that only weapons "designed for another purpose, an unacceptable purpose" were prohibited — no compensation or inventory-relief mechanism addressed

notes the new firearms regulations are controversial and unlikely to gain unanimous consent regardless, so asks why the government hasn't simply tabled the full legislative framework (including the buyback program) for first reading now, so the scope is clear; Blair commits to bringing forward legislation covering the buyback program and "a number of other significant measures" to strengthen gun control "at the first opportunity," framing the pandemic as not diminishing that responsibility, but without a specific date

cites a press release from Wet'suwet'en elected chiefs and community members stating they were excluded from "secret negotiations" on a memorandum of understanding affecting land rights/title, with only a few hereditary chiefs involved, and their request to halt a joint announcement scheduled for May 14 until the community can review it; asks whether the minister will agree to delay

Bennett's first answer emphasizes "ongoing" communication between "our partners," encourages continued Wet'suwet'en-led internal conversation, and frames the government's role as "giving them space," without a direct delay commitment

Schmale directly asks "is that a yes" to delaying until elected chiefs review; Bennett says she believes the elected chiefs "have had a look" at the agreement already, calling the underlying rights-and-title issues "very difficult conversations" that have been "outstanding for a long time" — again not directly confirming or denying a delay

Schmale argues the health crisis shouldn't be used to sideline the Wet'suwet'en people, cites the elected chiefs' escalation to calling for Bennett's resignation over the consultation failure, and asks for a process honoring both the traditional house system and elected governance; Bennett reiterates engagement "must take place and be led by the Wet'suwet'en nation," involving both elected and hereditary leadership jointly with Canada and BC

Schmale repeats the delay request a third time, citing continuing news reports that elected chiefs/community haven't had adequate review time; Bennett cites engagement "in the feast houses" and notification predating COVID as evidence work is underway, still framing the ultimate choice as Wet'suwet'en-led, no delay confirmed

Schmale alleges Liberal members on the indigenous-affairs committee have "shut down" Conservatives and witnesses "every time" the word "Wet'suwet'en" comes up for two weeks running, calling this inconsistent with the Liberals' claimed reconciliation advocacy; Bennett disagrees there's any intent to suppress discussion, reframes committee priority as addressing COVID-19 impacts on First Nations, Inuit, and Métis communities

Schmale repeats the shutdown allegation once more and asks when public debate will be allowed; Bennett defers to committee process/decision-making and reiterates the safety priority for Indigenous communities during COVID

Kusie opens by criticizing a 3-month delay before any seniors-specific announcement, asking why seniors are treated as an "afterthought"; Schulte cites ongoing seniors support since the pandemic began and announces, that same day, a one-time special payment for OAS recipients

Kusie details the toll — nearly two months of isolation, retirement-savings losses, added health precautions — before the ~$500 one-time payment; asks again why seniors are "consistently undervalued"; Schulte reminds her of an earlier GST top-up (~$375 for single seniors, over $500 for couples) as additional context to the day's announcement

Sgro (sharing time with Blois) highlights 30% of her riding (Humber River–Black Creek) being 65+, one of the highest-risk populations, citing added costs for medication, grocery delivery, and dispensing fees; asks what support is being provided

Schulte details the full package: $300 tax-free payment for OAS-eligible seniors, an additional $200 for GIS-eligible seniors (up to $500 total for the most vulnerable), plus $20M to expand the New Horizons for Seniors program funding grocery-delivery and social-connection initiatives, alongside the earlier GST credit
Sgro thanks the minister and requests continued work; Schulte thanks seniors and MPs for their advocacy and ongoing communication of needs
cites Abacus Data polling: 69% of Canadians expect a second wave, 52% perceive a PPE/medical-equipment shortage; asks for the government's second-wave PPE plan

Anand describes "aggressively buying" from a "diverse range" of domestic and international suppliers, scaling up domestic production, prioritizing front-line health workers currently, while exploring assistance for essential-service PPE needs more broadly, guided by public-health direction

Kusie cites specific PSPC fill-rate data: despite 1.8 billion total PPE units procured, under 6% of N95 respirator orders, under 8% of surgical mask orders, and just 1.4% of face-shield orders have actually been filled/delivered; asks what's causing the delay

Anand attributes delays to an "incredibly difficult and competitive global environment," cites daily procurement across multiple item types (face shields, gowns, hand sanitizer, N95/surgical masks, ventilators), and cites specific deliveries including "over two million face shields"

Kusie cites a University of Ottawa national-security expert calling the national emergency strategic stockpile a "failure," with Saskatchewan reportedly using expired PPE and Alberta using faulty PPE causing rashes/headaches, and notes ~34 of the government's suppliers are Chinese (a country already linked to faulty PPE shipments); asks what's being done to expedite procurement and screen out faulty supply

Anand cites multiple parallel supply chains (China, domestic Canadian production, the US, and other countries), reiterates the front-line-worker safety/effectiveness priority amid competitive global sourcing, and frames the effort as "ongoing" with "success" for front-line workers specifically

recalls a 10-weeks-earlier acknowledgment from the Minister of Fisheries that the lobster fishery faced up to 95% Asian-market losses, and a subsequent question (April 28) about harvesters left out of a $62.5M aid package (the minister had said she was "looking at sector-specific areas"); asks what the direct-support plan for seafood harvesters now looks like

Jordan confirms the sector's severe COVID impact, cites the $62.5M processor-focused package and CERB-eligibility changes covering seasonal workers and those who've exhausted fishery EI, acknowledges "more needs to be done" given the sector's "uniquely structured" enterprises, and says she's working with provincial and caucus colleagues

d'Entremont notes most fishing enterprises are family-run (spouses, sons, uncles, fathers, sometimes an entire family crew), making them ineligible for the wage subsidy's non-relative-employee rule, similar to farm enterprises; asks what direct financial help exists for these excluded operators

Jordan confirms the structural exclusion, reiterates the CERB changes made so far, and commits to "direct supports" being developed with cabinet colleagues, promising "more to say about that very soon"

raises a separately troubling development: an added catch-limitation/quota subsection quietly inserted into 2021 gulf-region lobster-licence conditions without advisory-member or harvester input, creating a "chill" in the fishery; asks how it was added without her authorization and whether it will recur
Jordan thanks those who flagged it, confirms it was "not done under my authorization," says it was "removed right away," and commits that "they will not happen"

recalls a February 26 exchange (following the CF-related death of 23-year-old Chantelle Lindsay) asking whether Trikafta would be made available; notes manufacturer Vertex Pharmaceuticals still hasn't applied to Health Canada nearly 12 weeks later, and that Conservative MPs sent a letter seeking an update on negotiations; asks when the drug will be available to CF patients

Hajdu expresses condolences to the Lindsay family, confirms Vertex hasn't applied, points to the special-access program as an interim path (majority of applicants have received access), and encourages continued correspondence with the manufacturer "as will we"

asks what's planned to help the Bar Harbor (Maine)–Yarmouth (Nova Scotia) ferry, used by tens of thousands of tourists, survive and resume service if borders stay closed through the summer; Joly cites prior conversations with him about Atlantic tourism-sector solutions and new ACOA (Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency) funding, offering to keep working with him and sector leaders

opens by thanking ministers/officials for support during Fort McMurray flooding; frames the sector's crisis as compounding years of prior pressure from Bill C-69 ("no more pipelines") and Bill C-48 (northern BC tanker ban), which he says pushed over $200B in investment out of Canada and pushed Alberta into recession even before COVID and the international oil price war; notes 48 days had passed since promised liquidity loans with no applications yet open, and asks when the government will act

O'Regan announces new large-cap liquidity measures that same day, describing them as completing an April 17 small/medium-business liquidity package (covering 85% of sector jobs); cites Canadian Association of Petroleum Producers praise that the new measures match what industry "asked for" and are needed for "future competitiveness"

Yurdiga notes junior oil companies closing, larger companies laying off contractors — many Indigenous-owned — struggling to qualify for existing aid programs; asks the Minister of Crown-Indigenous Relations (question directed there but answered by O'Regan) to close program gaps and review eligibility criteria for Indigenous business owners

O'Regan cites the sector's 576,000 total jobs, including 11,000 Indigenous jobs, particularly in Alberta/Saskatchewan, frames continued support as essential while balancing public-health/safety concerns in affected communities, without new specific program changes

Yurdiga raises the risk that if global oversupply persists into summer and production must shut down, thermal projects (e.g., SAGD) could be permanently lost, threatening long-term energy security; asks for the government's plan; O'Regan reiterates a worker- and job-retention-focused, industry/province-collaborative approach without new specifics on storage/shutdown risk

Yurdiga asks a technical eligibility question: does a mid-sized energy company already in default to financial institutions still qualify for the Business Credit Availability Program? O'Regan doesn't directly answer, reiterating the dual-crisis framing (COVID plus the global price war) and citing the April 17 and newly announced liquidity measures plus expanded BCAP eligibility generally

contrasts a newly announced $500M EDC loan to TC Energy for the Coastal GasLink pipeline (projected to produce 8.6 million tonnes of GHGs annually) against the entire forestry industry's $500M total EDC allocation under the 2017 softwood-lumber tariff action plan, despite forestry supporting 58,000 Quebec jobs and $6B of Quebec's GDP; calls this a "fundamental inequity" and asks the Minister of Natural Resources whether he considers it fair, and whether he'll commit to matching liquidity support for forestry

O'Regan (partly interrupted by an interpretation technical issue requiring the chair to pause proceedings) cites billions invested since 2017 including the softwood lumber action plan and strategic innovation fund forestry-specific support, describes spending "an inordinate amount of time" over the prior two-and-a-half months meeting forestry CEOs nationally (a recent coast-to-coast CEO convening specifically mentioned), and says the newly announced liquidity measures "will help some of them," without directly addressing the $500M-vs-$500M parity comparison

asks whether the government will show leadership on an interprovincial renewable-energy corridor to help sell competitively priced Quebec hydroelectricity (hard to sell "west of Quebec," e.g., in Ontario) to cut national emissions; Morneau gives only a general commitment to "continue working towards that end"

cites Canadian dairy processors facing 10-50% losses depending on product amid COVID and the new CUSMA agreement, and asks whether the government will commit to routing CUSMA import permits to processors rather than retailers directly; Freeland assures "fair compensation" for dairy producers and highlights preserving supply management in the renegotiated NAFTA, without addressing the processor-vs-retailer permit-allocation question

Gourde presses that processors specifically (who invest hundreds of millions annually and contribute $19B to GDP) are being asked to export value-added product while permits may favor "American multinationals," and repeats the processor-permit request; Freeland reiterates understanding of processors' role and a commitment to "continue to work with Canadian processors" as CUSMA takes effect, without a direct commitment

asks whether high-speed internet access (which he frames as determining who "fared better" financially during COVID) will be extended to all Canadians regardless of location; Monsef answers simply "Yes"

asks whether the government will invest in tourism infrastructure/upgrades so tourist regions are ready when the economy reopens; Joly answers "Yes," briefly interrupted by a channel-switching reminder from the chair, then elaborates a commitment to work with him and sector leaders on recovery

after opening remarks thanking House of Commons and constituency staff and describing King's-Hants' agricultural profile (largest concentration of producers east of Montreal, beef/wine/dairy/horticulture, the Kentville Research and Development Centre, and North America's longest-running agricultural exhibition), asks the Minister of Agriculture for an update specifically on dairy and horticulture support

Bibeau cites a $77.5M emergency processing fund (announced the prior Tuesday), a $50M surplus food program, $125M through AgriRecovery for beef and pork producers, an anticipated all-party-supported increase to dairy sector loan capacity (from $300M to $500M, expected the next day), and encourages farmers broadly to apply to business risk management programs including an improved AgriStability

cites a Pitt Meadows fitness-club owner ("Joel") facing 50-100% revenue drops whose landlord refuses to participate in the rent-assistance program despite the business needing only a 25% rent reduction; asks when government will help businesses whose landlords "refuse to be team players"

Morneau shares the concern, notes rent/landlord-tenant relations fall under provincial jurisdiction, says he regularly encourages provincial finance ministers to engage, and defends the program's design (up to 75% rent protection for landlords) as having "significant merit," while acknowledging enforcement requires provincial action

cites a beauty-salon owner ("Kathy") worried about meeting PPE requirements for BC's phased reopening; asks what the federal government is doing to ensure non-healthcare businesses can access PPE; Anand reiterates front-line-health-worker prioritization while describing active federal-provincial exploration of PPE access for "essential services and other businesses," without a specific mechanism or date
cites Wanstalls (the firearms retailer, described above) as a specific case of pandemic-plus-firearms-ban compounding hardship
cites the CERB $1,000-threshold repayment issue (described above) as a further concrete constituent concern

closes (after a point-of-order interruption, described below) with a question about farm labour: many farmers fear insufficient summer/fall workers; asks what the government is doing to make sure CERB/CESB recipients know about agri-food job opportunities; Qualtrough, with 15 seconds, assures that CERB/CESB support is paired with "creating tens of thousands of jobs, including in the agriculture sector," to ensure labour availability, without further specifics
Long-term care crisis and pharmacare (Davies, NDP)

describes conditions in Canadian long-term care homes as a national scandal — residents left in soiled clothing, going weeks without bathing, packed four to a room — severe enough that the Canadian Armed Forces had to be called in to intervene; asks the Minister of Health whether her government is "prepared to take strong action"

Hajdu calls the described conditions appalling, affirms seniors deserve to live with "dignity and safety," acknowledges this "just hasn't been happening" during COVID and, in some cases, before it; says she has publicly called for stronger long-term-care standards and has begun "preliminary conversations" with provincial/territorial counterparts and other ministers

Davies escalates with a comparison ("if we treated children the way we do seniors... social services would seize them"), cites that over 80% of Canadian COVID deaths have occurred in long-term care — the highest proportion among 14 comparable countries (including France, Germany, Denmark, Ireland) — and asks what specifically the minister will do

Hajdu notes long-term care sits mainly under provincial (and sometimes municipal) jurisdiction/funding, reiterates that ongoing federal-provincial-territorial conversations, including with subject-matter experts who've studied the issue repeatedly, are aimed at producing stronger standards, without a specific federal action

Davies rejects a "finger pointing" framing (attributing it implicitly to the minister's federalism point), reframes the crisis as the product of "decades of neglect" across all government levels exposed (not caused) by COVID; cites that no province/territory meets minimum hands-on-care standards, and that for-profit facilities show 2-3x the death rate of public/non-profit ones; asks whether the minister agrees on the need for national standards, funding tied to enforcement, and public delivery of care

Hajdu denies any finger-pointing on her part, characterizes provincial/territorial counterparts as willing collaborators both on immediate crisis response and longer-term "stronger network of long-term care or care alternatives," but offers no concrete new proposal, prompting Davies to note the absence of "a single concrete proposal or measure"

Davies pivots to pharmacare, noting millions of Canadians lost prescription-drug coverage tied to employment when they lost their jobs, exposing the fragility of employment-linked medical coverage; asks whether the government will "finally" implement universal pharmacare "at the earliest opportunity"; Hajdu confirms national pharmacare remains in her mandate letter from the Prime Minister ("I know it feels like a lifetime ago"), agrees the pandemic illustrates its importance, and commits to "continuing our work" without a timeline

cites a prior week's market shock caused by an economic-data leak before markets opened, calling the breach itself "unprecedented," and quotes Statistics Act s. 34 in full — criminalizing wilful disclosure or speculative use of market-moving information obtained through employment, with penalties up to a $5,000 fine or 5 years' imprisonment — and asks the minister directly whether the government considers this a criminal offence under that section, "yes or no"

Bains calls the breach "completely unacceptable," confirms the government has "denounced" it, notes Statistics Canada itself is "looking into this issue," and commits to preventing recurrence, without confirming or denying the criminal-offence characterization

Aboultaif interprets the response as an effective "yes" and asks whether the matter will therefore be "investigated"; Bains repeats that the breach "should not have occurred" and is "being looked into," again without confirming an investigation's formal status or authority

Aboultaif asks specifically whether Statistics Canada will investigate itself or whether the matter will be referred to the RCMP; after a brief audio-clarity interruption, Bains cites unspecified "appropriate protocols... in place to look into such breaches" that "will be followed," without naming StatsCan, an internal body, or the RCMP as the actual investigator

Aboultaif invokes the SNC-Lavalin affair, alleging Liberal staff refused to cooperate with that investigation, and asks for a commitment today that all Liberal staff will cooperate with this one; Bains reiterates the seriousness of the breach and commitment to "appropriate steps," without directly committing staff cooperation

on a final repeated yes/no push for that cooperation commitment, Bains falls back on "the process is very clear... the protocols are very clear... the law is very clear," again without an explicit yes
**Harrington Lake cottage and related items (Tochor, CPC)**

asks whether the government considers spousal reunification "essential travel" for border-entry purposes; Blair explains the CBSA exercises discretion over non-status individuals attempting non-essential entry, who are turned back under current restrictions — Tochor calls this "letting down Canadians," alleging people are being "stranded"

shifts to ask why the government didn't proactively disclose that the PM's official cottage (Harrington Lake) needed to be "rebuilt and massively expanded"; Anand explains the National Capital Commission (NCC), an independent Crown corporation, is restoring/maintaining official residences broadly, and that this information has been public "since 2018," denying any concealment

Tochor presses on whether there was "something in particular" being hidden, or whether "secrecy is all this government knows"; before Anand can respond, government House leader Rodriguez raises a point of order arguing the cottage question has "absolutely nothing to do with the pandemic" and is out of order; the chair (Stanton) agrees the committee's scope should relate to COVID but notes relevance can't be judged until a member has finished speaking, and asks Tochor to continue within those bounds, allowing him to finish the point (framed by Tochor as about transparency generally undermining pandemic-response trust) before moving on

pivots to ask who set the CERB amount at $2,000/month, contrasting it with the $1,200 seniors payment and $1,600 disability payment, and asking how those specific, seemingly ad hoc numbers were derived; Qualtrough explains ESDC and the Department of Finance worked collaboratively to determine an amount appropriate to anticipated worker income loss and living needs

closes by raising that charities/non-profits without their own payroll number are ineligible for the wage subsidy, and asks whether a program fix is coming; Hussen doesn't describe a wage-subsidy fix specifically, instead citing a separate $350M support package for charities/non-profits to continue and expand service to vulnerable Canadians through the pandemic

cites Michigan/Detroit as a pandemic epicentre (more Detroit deaths alone than the entire province of Ontario) and higher per-capita infection rates in border communities Windsor and Sarnia versus the rest of Ontario; notes the Canada-US border-restriction agreement expires the following week and that BC, Quebec, and Ontario premiers oppose reopening; asks whether restrictions will be extended or changed
Freeland says all border decisions prioritize Canadians' health/safety and that "very close conversations" with the US are underway regarding "next steps," without confirming extension or change

Masse asks directly what changes are "on the table"; Freeland declines specifics, describing a "collaborative conversation" rather than negotiation details, drawing on her NAFTA-negotiation experience that talks are "best not conducted in public"
Masse repeats the "any changes currently being discussed" question a third time; Freeland reiterates the cautious, collaborative-approach framing without new information

asks whether more data-sharing between Canadian and US governments on cross-border travelers is planned; Freeland says she's unsure what's being alluded to, but affirms current arrangements are "working extremely well" — non-essential travel sharply down, essential/trade travel continuing

asks whether border communities (given higher local infection rates) will get additional PPE/financial assistance tied to any "loosening" of restrictions; Freeland pushes back, noting Masse has "on a couple of occasions" implied a loosening is under discussion, which she explicitly says she has not stated

Masse pivots ("apparently we're meeting for nothing") to bank credit-card interest rates, calling large banks guilty of "profiteering" and "squeezing" Canadians at still-high, pre-pandemic "price-gouging" levels; cites Vancity Savings Credit Union's move to 0% credit-card rates as a model, and asks whether government will use its statutory powers to compel banks to match it

Morneau cites past work on interchange fees and, more recently, pandemic-era negotiated bank credit-card fee reductions and payment deferrals as evidence of progress, without addressing statutory compulsion
Masse repeats the "yes or no, will you use statutory powers" question a second time; Morneau reiterates ongoing work/negotiation with banks without a direct answer

asks why banks are permitted to profit from high interest/exchange rates on consumers and retailers specifically during COVID; Morneau clarifies banks have offered deferrals and cut interest "by half" for customers in trouble — Masse interjects "not on credit cards" — and Morneau clarifies that reduction applies "on credit cards" too

xi. on a final short question repeating the statutory-powers ask, Morneau again points to banks' 50% credit-card-fee cut as evidence of the government's approach working, without committing to compel further reductions
Green-recovery inconsistency and related exchange (Simard, BQ)

notes the PM's recent announcement of a green post-COVID economic-recovery plan, with Ministers Guilbeault, McKenna, and Wilkinson tasked to lead it, but expresses worry the group is "nothing but an empty shell" or "a convenient post-crisis political pitch," pointing to two major natural-resources announcements (the $1.7B orphan-well cleanup fund and, "yesterday," a $500M EDC loan to TC Energy for Coastal GasLink, projected to emit 8.6 million tonnes of GHGs annually) as evidence the government's actual resourcing skews fossil-fuel; asks how this squares with a green-transition ambition

Wilkinson responds that the immediate focus is on food/rent security and provincial reopening measures, that future-economy/climate conversations are needed "as we move forward," but that "at the current time, the focus is clearly on combatting the virus" — an answer partly disrupted by a translation/interpretation failure flagged via point of order by Ms. Pauzé, requiring the chair to pause and ask Wilkinson to repeat himself, which he does in similar terms
Simard follows with the forestry-parity comparison (detailed above under sector-specific support), receiving a similarly non-committal answer from O'Regan

a related procedural dispute follows: Brunelle-Duceppe raises a point of order arguing that Simard, a French-speaking member, lost roughly 45 seconds of his allotted 5 minutes due to the technical/interpretation delay and the need for a minister to repeat an answer, and that French-speaking members "shouldn't get the short end of the stick"; the chair says the clock had been stopped and commits to reviewing recorded footage to confirm; Brunelle-Duceppe insists time was lost regardless and asks that Simard be allowed one further question for fairness; the chair commits only to "check what happened" and find "a solution for next time"; Guilbeault raises a further point of order pushing back on any implication that members making an effort to answer in French were "unduly dragging out" time, framing that effort positively; the chair discourages the exchange from becoming a language-policy debate and returns the floor to Dalton with roughly 30 seconds remaining (used for the farm-labour question described above)

frames a "higher-level abstraction" question to the Prime Minister: given the global, "all-consuming" push for a vaccine and questions raised by Dr. Matthew Herder (Health Law Institute, Dalhousie) about the power structure and profit motive behind vaccine development — noting Jonas Salk famously never patented his polio vaccine — asks whether Canada can ensure publicly funded vaccine research results in a product shared "globally, openly, and not for profit"

Bains (answering for the PM) describes an "open science model," collaborative work with multiple partners/jurisdictions on vaccines and therapeutics, while adding that Canadian-developed IP will still be supported where it's "Canadian ingenuity" driving it

May follows up citing an allegation (from the same Dalhousie institute) that a for-profit motive delayed development of a Winnipeg-developed Ebola vaccine, as pharmaceutical companies waited to assess market interest before committing; asks whether the profit motive in vaccine/drug development is being actively examined as a policy question

Bains says he's working closely with Minister Hajdu and the Chief Science Advisor "to look at all options," highlights that the Ebola vaccine was itself developed in Canada and that SARS DNA sequencing was also done domestically as points of scientific pride, and commits to "continue to share details... with the public," without confirming a specific profit-motive policy review

May pivots to ask why the controversial firearms regulations (limiting "military-style assault rifles") haven't been fast-tracked as legislation, suggesting it's clearly because they wouldn't gain unanimous consent, and asks whether the government would table the full legislative framework — covering the buyback program and other elements — for first reading so the long-term picture is clear; Blair commits to bringing forward buyback and other gun-control legislation "at the first opportunity," reiterating that the pandemic doesn't diminish the government's responsibility to act, without a specific date (echoing his earlier answer to Schmale/Bergen on the same theme)

May separately raises disappointment with that morning's seniors announcement as insufficient, then narrows to well-run not-for-profit seniors' homes that, despite not losing revenue, face rising wage and PPE costs with "nowhere to look for help"; asks whether assistance is coming for that specific gap

Hajdu thanks long-term-care workers broadly, acknowledges the cost pressures May describes, and points to "generous transfers" to provinces/territories for health systems (to be allocated as provinces see fit) and ongoing conversations at the health ministers' table, without a targeted program for well-run non-profit homes specifically — the chair then cuts the exchange short for time

the chair (having earlier handed proceedings to acting chair Bruce Stanton for portions of the session) closes by thanking all members for consistently wearing headsets throughout — noting no one answered without one, benefiting both fellow members and interpreters — and expresses personal pride in the day's session before adjourning the committee until noon the next day
