non_verbatim_nodes.text: none today; sixth meeting of the special committee, held by videoconference
McPherson — a national perinatal mental health strategy (screening, funding, treatment access)
Reid — rescind Patented Medicine Prices Review Board changes threatening access to cystic-fibrosis drug Trikafta
May — address the severe family-doctor shortage, especially rural
Vis — stop targeting law-abiding firearms owners, redirect funds to anti-gang enforcement and CBSA smuggling interdiction
Johns — ban expansion of open-net salmon farming in Nova Scotia, invest in closed-containment aquaculture instead
Manly — halt Coastal GasLink construction on Wet'suwet'en territory pending nation-to-nation talks
Ratansi — withhold airline financial assistance until cancelled-flight refunds are issued
presses Trudeau to confirm reports that federal staff were told to ignore ~200,000 applications flagged as potentially fraudulent

asks repeatedly (6+ times) whether the PM or his office signed off on the deputy-minister memo; Trudeau never answers directly, repeating that speed to help Canadians was the priority and cleanup/audits would follow
asks whether every individual fraud case will be investigated; Trudeau commits only in general terms to "clean up after the fact"
asks the Minister of National Revenue directly whether a CRA memo told employees to ignore detected fraud and still send CERB payments; Lebouthillier answers "no" outright

separately presses (4+ times) for a simple answer on CERB repayment mechanics for a worker who returns to work mid-month — $500/week or the full $2,000; Qualtrough says it depends on individual circumstances and Service Canada will work case-by-case, never giving the requested number

asks whether an employee can still refuse to return to work (and keep CERB) if an employer meets hygiene requirements; Qualtrough cites existing labour-refusal processes and says CERB is for those not working due to COVID

welcomes the Large Employer Emergency Financing Facility's anti-tax-evasion condition, then notes it targets only abusive/illegal evasion, not legal tax-haven avoidance used by banks and multinationals; asks why "profiteers" using legal avoidance still qualify

asks whether a bank relocating its most profitable Canadian activities to a subsidiary in a tax haven counts as paying its fair share; Trudeau says applications will be assessed case-by-case for transparency, and that big banks aren't expected to need the funds

separately raises interchange (credit-card) fees at 2.5-3%, nearly 10x Europe/Australia's, hurting merchants; asks Trudeau to cap them at 0.3% as those regions did; Trudeau deflects to consumer-support measures generally, without addressing the merchant-fee cap

cites a Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives report (top-100 CEOs earned 227x average workers in 2018, CEO pay up 18% vs. ~flat real wage growth) and past Quebec political consensus (post-Bombardier) for capping exec pay tied to state aid; asks for a clear commitment to a ceiling; Morneau confirms conditions are coming (no dividends/share buybacks, executive-compensation limits, tax-structure review) but gives no specific cap figure, promising "more details in coming days"

cites a single parent of four who lost spousal/child support due to COVID but is ineligible for CERB (pays tax on spousal income); notes the Minister of Employment has known for three weeks with no fix; Trudeau cites expanded CCB payments as a partial answer, not directly addressing the spousal-support gap

argues the federal homelessness response is inadequate for social distancing/hygiene needs, especially in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside SROs; asks for matching funds for permanent post-COVID housing solutions; Trudeau cites hundreds of millions already sent to shelters and the national housing strategy's 50% chronic-homelessness reduction goal

counters that a 50%-reduction goal isn't good enough and that the Downtown Eastside's large urban Indigenous population received under 2% of pandemic urban-Indigenous-housing funding despite being overrepresented among the homeless; Trudeau acknowledges "more to do" without a specific commitment

notes CERB rules require repaying the full $2,000 if a recipient earns over $1,000 in a period, creating a disincentive/trap for part-time workers who slightly exceed the threshold; Qualtrough says the $1,000 earning allowance was already a relaxation from an initial no-work rule, and Service Canada will work with individuals to avoid undue hardship, without resolving the cliff-edge design

cites a constituent whose documents (including a doctor's note) sent March 12 were never opened, forcing a resend; Hussen says he's not aware this is widespread, offers to look into the specific case, cites redeployed staff and pandemic-driven office closures

challenges banning the Iver Johnson single-shot rifle, a common inherited farm gun, arguing front-line officers are focused on gangs/smuggling, not farmers/hunters; Blair cites the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police and Ontario police leaders' public support for banning "military-design" rifles as the basis for the list, and notes any gun-violence death is "one too many"; Bergen counters by invoking the costly, ineffective long-gun registry precedent

cites a Maple Ridge retailer (Wanstalls, 8 employees) stuck with unsellable banned-firearm inventory; Blair reiterates that hunting/sport-shooting weapons remain legal, only weapons "designed for combat" were prohibited

asks why the full legislative framework (including the buyback program) hasn't been tabled for first reading, given it clearly won't gain unanimous consent anyway; Blair commits to bringing it forward "at the first opportunity" alongside other gun-control measures, without a date

cites elected Wet'suwet'en chiefs' press release asking to delay the May 14 rights-and-title MOU announcement until the community has reviewed it, alleging only hereditary chiefs were consulted in "secret negotiations"

presses repeatedly for a direct delay commitment; Bennett says engagement must be "Wet'suwet'en-led," involving both elected and hereditary leadership, and that consultation (feast-house engagement) predates COVID — never confirms or denies a delay

cites elected chiefs calling for Bennett's resignation over the process, and alleges the indigenous-affairs committee has repeatedly shut down Conservative attempts to raise the Wet'suwet'en issue; Bennett disputes any intent to suppress debate, reframes the priority as protecting Indigenous communities from COVID
Kusie criticizes a 3-month delay before announcing seniors support, calling seniors an "afterthought"; Schulte cites a new one-time $500 OAS payment plus an earlier ~$375-$500 GST top-up

Sgro (sharing time with Blois) highlights rising costs for seniors (medication, grocery delivery, dispensing fees); Schulte details the breakdown — $300 for OAS recipients, additional $200 for GIS recipients (up to $500 total), plus $20M for the New Horizons for Seniors program (grocery delivery, staying connected)

cites survey data (69% expect a second wave, 52% perceive a PPE shortage), asks about second-wave PPE readiness; Anand cites aggressive global/domestic procurement, prioritizing front-line health workers

cites fill-rates from Public Services and Procurement Canada — under 6% of N95 orders, under 8% of surgical masks, 1.4% of face shields delivered against 1.8B units ordered; Anand cites a difficult competitive global market and cites specific deliveries (2M+ face shields)

cites a University of Ottawa security expert calling the national stockpile a failure, plus expired PPE used in Saskatchewan and faulty (rash/headache-causing) PPE in Alberta, and notes ~34 suppliers are Chinese; Anand cites multiple parallel supply chains (China, domestic, US, other countries) prioritizing safety for front-line workers

cites a 95% Asian-market loss for lobster exporters and a $62.5M aid package that left harvesters out; asks for a harvester-specific plan; Jordan cites CERB eligibility expansions for seasonal/fishery-EI-exhausted workers and ongoing work with provinces, acknowledges "more needs to be done"

notes most fishing enterprises are family-run and thus excluded from the wage subsidy's non-relative-employee rule; Jordan confirms this gap and says direct-support measures are being developed, "hopefully" with news soon
raises an unauthorized quota/catch-limit regulation quietly added to 2021 gulf-region lobster licences without consultation; Jordan confirms it was not authorized by her and has been removed

notes ~12 weeks since a constituent's CF-related death and that manufacturer Vertex still hasn't applied to Health Canada; Hajdu confirms this, points to the special-access program (majority of applicants approved) as an interim path, encourages continued correspondence with Vertex
asks about support for the Bar Harbor-Yarmouth ferry if borders stay closed; Joly commits to working with him via ACOA funding, no specifics

cites Bill C-69/C-48 and the COVID/price-war double hit on Alberta's oil sector, and that liquidity loans promised 48 days earlier still had no applications open; O'Regan announces new large-cap liquidity measures that day, building on earlier small/medium-business measures (April 17, covering 85% of sector jobs)

asks about Indigenous oil-and-gas contractors (many laid off) struggling to qualify for aid; O'Regan cites ~576,000 sector jobs including 11,000 Indigenous workers and general ongoing support, without new specific measures

asks about the risk of permanently losing thermal (SAGD) storage/production capacity if oversupply forces shutdowns; O'Regan reiterates a worker-focused, industry-collaborative approach without new specifics

asks whether a company in default to financial institutions still qualifies for the Business Credit Availability Program; O'Regan doesn't directly answer, reiterating the April 17 and newly announced liquidity measures

contrasts a $500M EDC loan for TC Energy's Coastal GasLink pipeline (8.6M tonnes CO2/year) against the entire forestry sector's $500M EDC allocation during the 2017 softwood-lumber tariff response, despite forestry supporting 58,000 Quebec jobs and $6B of GDP; asks if this is fair and for matching liquidity for forestry; O'Regan cites past softwood-lumber and strategic-innovation-fund investment plus recent CEO consultations, without directly addressing the funding-parity comparison
asks for a renewable-energy transmission corridor to sell Quebec hydro power to other provinces; Morneau gives only a general "continuing to work towards that"

cites 10-50% losses for Canadian dairy processors amid CUSMA, asks for import permits to go to processors rather than retailers; Freeland cites preserving supply management in the new NAFTA without addressing the processor-permit request directly
asks if government will invest in universal rural high-speed internet; Monsef answers "yes"
asks if government will invest in tourism infrastructure for reopening; Joly answers "yes" and commits to working with him

asks for an update on dairy and horticulture support; Bibeau cites a $77.5M emergency processing fund, $50M surplus food program, $125M AgriRecovery for beef/pork, a proposed dairy loan-capacity increase from $300M to $500M pending all-party support, and encourages AgriStability applications

cites a fitness-club owner whose landlord refuses the rent-assistance program despite steep revenue losses; Morneau notes rent relief is provincial jurisdiction, encourages provincial enforcement, defends the program's design (up to 75% landlord protection)
cites a beauty-salon owner worried about PPE access for reopening; Anand cites front-line-worker prioritization while "actively" exploring provincial/business PPE access, no firm commitment
asks how CERB/CESB recipients will learn about agri-food job openings amid labour shortage fears; Qualtrough cites job-creation efforts including in agriculture, without specifics
Long-term care crisis and pharmacare (Davies, NDP)

describes severe long-term-care conditions (soiled clothing, weeks without bathing, overcrowding) that required military intervention; asks if the government will take strong action; Hajdu calls the situation unacceptable, cites preliminary conversations toward stronger national standards

cites 80%+ of Canadian COVID deaths occurring in long-term care — the highest share among 14 comparable countries; Hajdu notes care homes are primarily provincial/municipal jurisdiction, reiterates ongoing intergovernmental conversations

cites no province/territory meeting minimum hands-on care standards and 2-3x higher death rates in for-profit vs. public/non-profit homes; asks for national standards, funding tied to enforcement, and public delivery of care; Hajdu denies "finger-pointing," cites provincial willingness to collaborate but offers no concrete proposal

pivots to pharmacare, noting millions lost prescription coverage when they lost jobs; asks for universal pharmacare "at the earliest opportunity"; Hajdu confirms it remains in her mandate, commits only to "continuing the work"

cites a pre-market-open economic data leak and Statistics Act penalties (s. 34) for improper disclosure/use of market-moving information; asks whether the government considers it a criminal offence under that section; Bains calls the breach "completely unacceptable" and says it's "being looked into," without confirming the criminal-offence characterization
presses on whether Statistics Canada will investigate itself or the matter will go to the RCMP; Bains cites unspecified "appropriate protocols" without naming an investigator

invokes the SNC-Lavalin affair's staff non-cooperation as a precedent concern, asks for a commitment that Liberal staff will cooperate with this investigation; Bains reiterates process/protocol language without a direct commitment
asks about spousal-reunification travel being classified as essential for border entry; Blair says CBSA exercises discretion, non-essential entries by non-status individuals are turned back

questions why the government didn't proactively disclose the scale of Harrington Lake cottage rebuilding/expansion; Anand says the NCC (an independent Crown corporation) has managed this as part of broader official-residence restoration, information public since 2018
a point of order from the government House leader challenges the relevance of the cottage question to the pandemic's scope; the chair asks members to stay on topic but lets the exchange continue

asks who set the CERB amount at $2,000 and how disability/senior benefit amounts were derived; Qualtrough says ESDC and Finance jointly determined the figure based on anticipated lost employment income

asks about a fix for charities/non-profits without their own payroll number being ineligible for the wage subsidy; Hussen cites a separate $350M support fund for charities rather than a wage-subsidy fix

cites Michigan/Detroit's outbreak severity and higher infection rates in border communities (Windsor, Sarnia), asks whether Canada-US border restrictions (expiring the following week) will be extended; Freeland says decisions prioritize Canadian health/safety and cites "close conversations" with the US without confirming an extension
presses repeatedly on what specific changes are under discussion; Freeland declines to detail ongoing negotiations, reiterating a cautious, collaborative approach
asks whether border communities will get added PPE/financial support if restrictions loosen; Freeland pushes back on the premise that loosening is being discussed

pivots to credit-card interest rates, citing Vancity's move to 0% as a model, and asks whether government will use statutory powers to force banks to match it; Morneau cites past interchange-fee negotiations and pandemic-era bank rate cuts/deferrals, declines to commit to compelling banks by statute

Simard's forestry-parity question (above) sits alongside a broader challenge that the government's promised green post-COVID recovery task force (Guilbeault/McKenna/Wilkinson) looks like "an empty shell" given fossil-fuel-heavy announcements (e.g., $1.7B for orphan-well cleanup, the $500M Coastal GasLink EDC loan); Wilkinson says the immediate focus remains COVID relief, with climate/future-economy conversations to come "as we move beyond this phase," and technical interpretation issues briefly interrupt this exchange (raised by a point of order)

citing Dr. Matthew Herder (Dalhousie) and Jonas Salk's unpatented polio vaccine as precedent, asks whether publicly funded vaccine research will be shared openly/non-commercially rather than patented for profit; Bains cites an "open science" collaborative model while noting Canadian IP will still be supported

cites an allegation that a for-profit motive delayed a Winnipeg-developed Ebola vaccine, asks if the profit motive in drug development is under review; Bains cites ongoing work with Hajdu and the chief science advisor, highlighting Canadian contributions (Ebola vaccine, SARS sequencing) without committing to a specific policy review
meeting closes with the chair thanking members for consistent headset use (aiding interpreters) and expressing pride in the session; committee adjourns until noon the next day

non_verbatim_nodes.text: Children, Young People and Education Committee (Welsh Senedd); apologies from Suzy Davies and Hefin David, no substitutions
Chair Lynne Neagle declares she chairs the cross-party group on suicide prevention, for which Samaritans Cymru (appearing later) provides the secretariat
agenda item 2: an evidence session for the committee's inquiry on education otherwise than at school (EOTAS)
Session 1: local-authority panel (Sharon Davies, Torfaen/ADEW; Nick Williams, Swansea/ADEW; David Hopkins, WLGA)

Williams: more prevalent, very challenging behaviour across the system, often tied to ASD (autism spectrum disorder) and difficulty securing the right provision; Swansea's relevant numbers have risen roughly fourfold over five-six years; what looks like difficult behaviour is often additional learning needs, and system capacity hasn't caught up, pressuring both schools and EOTAS/PRU capacity
Davies: Torfaen sees the same pattern and "seconds" Williams's account

Williams: Swansea has developed a new behaviour-and-well-being strategy with a tiered/staged approach including universal provision; similar strategies exist regionally (south-west and mid Wales) and, per the EOTAS network he chairs nationally, in many other local authorities; the direction has "moved forward" over the past two-three years but there's "a little bit of lag" bringing every authority to a consistent level
some learners will always need more specialist provision beyond what mainstream staff/schools can be equipped to deliver

Davies: schools face "a huge amount of pressures... to perform," and school culture plays into exclusion trends; interim measures (i.e., the shift toward the capped-9 attainment measure) are producing a cultural shift, but she expects "a lag in the system" before effects show up for learners; Torfaen has been "working really hard" on exclusions and ensuring a broad, balanced curriculum for every learner

Williams (answering partly in Welsh): the messages government and local-authority directors/councils send matter — emphasizing children's future progression, not just reaching a fixed attainment level; Estyn itself has "changed its mind" and updated its messaging, and schools now better understand what's expected of them

Williams: Swansea/Neath Port Talbot use a "team-around-the-family" approach, bringing multiple agencies together proactively, recognizing that behaviours seen at school usually run deeper in the home environment, requiring a whole-family support lens

Davies and Williams agree the majority of Welsh local authorities now share this multi-agency understanding, working alongside social care and health colleagues on the "whole package" around families and learners

Williams: extensive training across Wales on adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) and trauma-informed practice has changed how staff interpret behaviour — he recalls that as a teacher himself, he previously saw only "difficult behaviours" without understanding the background driving them; the profession is "more informed" now
**Funding (questions from Siân Gwenllian, with Sian Hughes)**

Davies: the incoming Additional Learning Needs (ALN) Act will add pressure to an already-stretched system; some Torfaen schools are behind on funding and forced into "hard choices" across every aspect of provision for learners
Davies isn't sure ALN specifically is "worse affected" than other areas, but agrees more spending will likely be needed in light of the new Act; Williams agrees

Williams: government funding announcements sometimes overlook PRU staff specifically, who may need even more training than mainstream school staff — government has since "addressed that" after being pushed, but it remains "a little bit of an afterthought," with more attention needed going forward

Hopkins (WLGA), on delegation of funding to schools: delegation levels are "already very high" in most authorities, with agreements in place with government to devolve as much funding to schools as possible — he doesn't see delegation itself as a direct driver of exclusions; instead, he points to the narrow key-stage-4 end-point attainment measure as pressuring some headteachers toward exclusion or moving pupils to another school (which he calls "regrettable"), and separately flags that ALN funding is coming under increasing pressure — citing England's parallel legislative experience, where ALN-related tribunals became so burdensome that local authorities there "almost gave up going to tribunals" after repeatedly losing

Hopkins on whether new-Act pressures could mean more exclusions: "it shouldn't, but it could," depending on how headteachers/governing bodies react to financial and performance pressure; he hopes the new curriculum, alongside efforts with Estyn and Welsh Government to broaden accountability measures beyond narrow metrics, will let schools approach this more constructively; separately flags that ALN legislation extends support obligations up to age 25, adding pressure across the post-16 sector too

Davies: variable, unpredictable provision needs (changing term to term, even week to week, as learners move in and out) make planning difficult and strain budgets that weren't allocated for unplanned arrivals

Williams: PRUs have worked to ensure funding "follows" a child who moves out of mainstream school, since funding is only allocated annually, creating a lag risk when a school no longer educates a child but still holds that year's funding
**Collaborative working and transition arrangements (questions from Janet Finch-Saunders)**

Williams: PRU-sector networking has improved substantially — national PRU meetings, a regionally meeting EOTAS group, shared-practice conferences, joint provision visits, and closer curriculum-focused work between PRU and mainstream staff, aided by opportunities the new curriculum presents (contingent on funding and time); historically, staff sometimes lacked cross-setting experience in either direction

on transition from PRU back to mainstream: Williams describes constituency-level problems where children can end up stuck at home between settings; Swansea has invested significant time and (via Band B capital funding) is building a brand-new PRU, opening January 2021; staff work closely with schools, using a part-time-timetable integration process with continued support after full return, gradually reduced — "proven very successful," though he's candid that reintegration becomes "far, far more difficult" for the most challenging, oldest (key-stage-4) learners, who are instead supported toward further education/college transitions

Davies: Torfaen similarly leans on the team-around-the-family approach for reintegration, considering the "whole package" around a learner — including transport — to prepare everything needed for a successful return where possible; agrees key stage 4 is hardest

Hopkins: at least one (unnamed — he says he's "not allowed to say") local authority is exploring retaining all pupils within mainstream school settings entirely; it's "early days," the principle is appealing but raises other funding/administrative issues; a similar model has been tried in England (Oxfordshire), though long-term outcomes there aren't well known to WLGA

Davies (drawing on her earlier career as an English primary headteacher): recalls Oxfordshire specifically considered dissolving its PRU and returning the money to secondary schools under a partnership arrangement with terms of reference (short of a formal service-level agreement), preventing schools from simply moving learners around; it "started off really well" some years ago, though she doesn't know if it continued

Williams: Swansea has run a similar "devolve" (not "delegate," a distinction he stresses) model for almost three years, giving secondary schools extra resource plus a monitored action plan for how they use it — while conceding some learners will always need additional, bespoke support beyond what schools can provide; he calls Swansea's overall approach "a mixed economy"

Williams: capacity — insufficient spaces in some year groups — is the core cause; robust panels/systems try to ensure everything possible is attempted within the home school first, sometimes via a (non-ideal, but family-and-youngster-informed) part-time timetable; Swansea has "reinvigorated" its managed-move program (with a dedicated overseer working closely with secondary schools) to give learners a genuine "second chance," including a cooling-off period if a learner prefers their original school — learner voice is treated as important, requiring "quite wide" provision options

Williams: local authorities already run such frameworks, constrained by a shortage of additional providers and the priority placed on safeguarding — a "balancing act" between rigor and not discouraging providers from coming forward; beyond safeguarding, training/support for staff in that additional provision remains "a struggle" given existing capacity pressures on in-house provision and oversight visits
**Local-authority awareness and quality assurance of school-organized EOTAS**
Williams (Swansea only): schools must report EOTAS-provision locations as part of a required plan, and challenge advisers monitor/quality-assure this during school visits
on safeguarding of privately run/independent EOTAS: Williams affirms schools take safeguarding "very, very seriously" as a "prime driver," though he can't speak beyond Swansea

on local-authority quality-assurance role for school-organized EOTAS: Williams notes much additional provision (e.g., a mechanics course via a college) is also used directly by the local authority itself, so it gets "quality assured... by two sides"

Davies: Torfaen's secondary schools run their own Torfaen Curriculum Panel (TCP) reviewing alternative provision, attended by senior leaders, currently undergoing a review of whether provision that worked in the past still fits current, more complex learner needs, whether providers still offer what's sought, whether the curriculum offer and staff training are right, and generally "keeping that momentum going" rather than assuming past success guarantees present fitness
**Individual/home tuition quality assurance (clarified as meaning home tuition specifically, per the chair)**
Davies: local authorities are legally "restricted" in how much access they get into a family's home, making quality assurance difficult unless families themselves invite them in

Williams: Swansea uses only local-authority-employed home-tuition staff (never agency staff) for children who, for reasons like school anxiety or medical need, currently can't access school or approved provision — he doesn't know if this is standard practice across Wales, only for Swansea; Davies confirms Torfaen is "very similar"

Hopkins: historically, directly provided/commissioned home tuition would be quality-assured as a matter of course; the harder question is other, third-party-commissioned forms of provision, where commissioning arrangements should require quality safeguards but monitoring is the real challenge — he can't give a definitive Wales-wide answer
**WLGA paper concern on EOTAS pupil registration changes**

Williams (on a joint ADEW/WLGA paper flagging concern about "potential impact of changes to the registration of pupils who are EOTAS" for data/funding/joint working): stresses the importance of funding following the learner and of schools retaining "shared ownership," since EOTAS placement is meant to be temporary and reintegration-focused for most learners; connects this to the committee's earlier questions about "off-rolling" at GCSE stage to keep pupils out of school performance data, which local-authority messaging (to governors, headteachers, staff) actively works against — framing EOTAS learners as "our learners," the "most vulnerable" the system has, with direct links (if unsupported) to crime and broader societal cost, making it "in all our interests" to do right by them
**Curriculum access and consistency (questions from Siân Gwenllian)**

Hopkins: distinguishes PRUs (which follow a set, inspected curriculum under local-authority control — WLGA is "happy and content" there) from local-authority-commissioned home tuition (which should have safeguards, though what actually happens in the home can't always be guaranteed) from third-party-commissioned provision (hardest to vouch for — commissioning terms should require quality safeguards, but monitoring is the open question); calls this "very general, broad-brush" and defers specifics to his co-panelists
asked directly whether this variability worries the WLGA, Hopkins confirms: "of course it's a concern... if you can't guarantee quality in any shape or form for a young person"

Williams: regional collaboration on staff training (including joint work with school staff) is "quite positive," though "there is work to do"; PRUs currently deliver broad-and-balanced curriculum by requirement, including literacy, numeracy, and Welsh — learners aren't "out all the time"
Davies: reiterates collaboration between PRUs and schools as the key mechanism for ensuring learners get what they need

Gwenllian presses that this describes best practice under direct local-authority control, but asks about inconsistency beyond PRUs (home/private provision) — whether the panel is presenting only the "best elements" while under-the-surface problems go unexamined; Williams responds that "consistency is developing across Wales" in curriculum and collaboration terms — not perfect, but improving

Bowden raises Hopkins's earlier ALN point directly: is ALN support especially hard to secure in EOTAS settings specifically, since EOTAS learners often have particular needs that make EOTAS placement necessary in the first place?

Hopkins: within tightly regulated settings (PRUs, local-authority-commissioned/delivered tuition), needs "definitely should be being met," though he can't confirm they all are; outside that tightly regulated part of the system, meeting individual needs becomes "increasingly difficult" — he flags this as a likely genuine issue, deferring to colleagues for more detail

Bowden presses further: there's a known "disconnect" between what should happen and what does — even within local-authority PRUs, the full curriculum (beyond basic numeracy/literacy/well-being) isn't always delivered, and provision quality varies even in commissioned EOTAS settings
Hopkins: variation exists, but within the local-authority-maintained sector, provision "should be being made," and if not, the local authority should be aware and address it

Williams: references Swansea's own inspection history — provision that fell short "some years ago" now inspects "very positive," though he stresses "we're not being complacent"; the biggest ongoing challenge is capacity, tied to funding — he'd like a dedicated educational psychologist working solely with PRU/EOTAS learners, but current system-wide demand doesn't allow it

Davies: agrees capacity is central but stresses it's also about retaining the *right* staff — specialist expertise (built over years) is "quite niche," and when an expert person moves on or retires, rebuilding that capability "from scratch" is genuinely difficult; it's "more than just one person," requiring a whole surrounding training package

Williams: proposes building EOTAS/PRU exposure into initial teacher training (currently, newly qualified teachers can't work directly in this provision — arguably reasonable, since they should establish mainstream experience first, but a future specialist pipeline is still needed) and into ongoing professional development, with two-way exchange (PRU staff visiting schools and vice versa) to counter the professional isolation that can come with long PRU tenures; flags this as a discussion topic for the EOTAS network he chairs

Bowden references prior Estyn evidence about small PRU staff numbers limiting access to professional training, and asks if that matches the panel's experience and what could be done; Davies: the picture is "limited" but "getting better," citing growing networks and conferences

Bowden asks whether local authorities can encourage specialist staff (teachers, educational psychologists) to share expertise with independent EOTAS providers; Williams: again a capacity conundrum — pulling specialists out of provision is hard to backfill (e.g., via supply teachers) given existing demands
Davies: suggests creating an explicit specialization pathway/offer for staff who want to move further into this area, which currently doesn't formally exist

Williams: mental-health-service access varies even within his own region, which spans three separate health boards; his own region's access "hasn't been great, to be honest," though a positive step is the new requirement for each health board to have a "DECLO" (designated education clinical lead officer — Williams can't recall the exact term on the spot), with whom his authority has already met; he expects stronger future partnerships, alongside the local authority's own universal well-being strategy (including counselling) designed to reach learners appropriately at different stages without over-referring

Bowden asks whether a lack of mainstream mental-health support could itself be pushing more learners toward EOTAS; Hopkins: suspects a "general deficit" in Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services (CAMHS) capacity broadly (not a criticism of the service itself, just its scale), which likely translates into pressure on learners with additional needs regardless of setting — though he has no direct evidence base to offer
**Teacher training and workforce sustainability (Siân Gwenllian supplementary)**

Gwenllian asks whether new teachers, even without direct EOTAS training, are otherwise equipped to handle rising challenging behaviour generally, given how many leave the profession over exactly this; suggests the system needs a more holistic response

Williams: attributes attrition to more than challenging behaviour alone — notes increased school placement time for trainees now helps, alongside needing both theory and mentored practice, plus consistent school-wide behaviour policy
Gwenllian: presses that losing experienced staff while fewer enter the profession compounds the "bigger picture" challenge; Davies agrees ("Yes, certainly")
chair notes her understanding that the CAMHS in-reach project operating in Gwent doesn't include PRUs, and asks Davies to confirm; Davies isn't sure

chair separately asks about the Gwent attachment team's work with PRUs and its impact on staff support/embedding trauma awareness; Davies: any professional learning is positive, calling it "positive impact" though "early days" and the "overall impact" isn't yet known

Williams: cites Powys as an example — provision spans from near Oswestry in the north to Ystradgynlais in the south, with separate north/south PRU provision but still enormous travel distances for learners; contrasts this with more geographically compact Torfaen, where he'd guess (deferring to Davies) transport is less of an issue
Hopkins: not personally aware of transport issues but hasn't specifically investigated, and is open to looking into it
the chair thanks the panel, notes some areas will follow up by letter, confirms a transcript will be sent for accuracy review, and calls a break before the second session
Session 2: Samaritans / Mind Cymru panel (Sarah Stone, Samaritans Cymru; Liz Williams, Samaritans; Dr Ian Johnson, Mind Cymru) — sixth evidence session of the inquiry

Johnson: calls this "a very difficult subject" given limited visibility into underlying reasons; statistical releases give only reductionist categories (persistent disruptive behaviour, verbal abuse, physical assaults) without the deeper causal story, even though (drawing on his own experience as a recent primary/secondary school governor) schools generate a substantial paper trail before any exclusion — that detail "doesn't seem to really find its way up to a higher level"

on rising exclusions among younger children specifically: Johnson finds this "very concerning" and notes a substantial recent increase, but the supporting evidence remains largely anecdotal (behavioural/underlying issues, growing ACEs awareness); he can't yet explain why primary schools specifically appear to be excluding more

Stone: Samaritans' original report on school exclusions began from anecdotal reports of individual distress reaching the charity via projects working with excluded young people, including primary-school-age children; the report's central message is that this raises "serious questions" the sector "doesn't know the answer" to without dedicated further work, given the impact on affected young people's life trajectories

Johnson: cites Estyn's pupil-registration-practices report (October of the prior year) on off-rolling — a "strong impact" specifically between year 10 and 11 (~4% of pupils off-rolled), alongside a steadier baseline of 1.5-2% off-rolled in other transition years (year 8/9, year 9/10); based on cohorts of roughly 30,000-32,000, that steadier rate implies 500-600 children off-rolled in any given year outside the year-10/11 spike — a pattern he calls concerning specifically because of its "normalisation" throughout the secondary system; calls the existing Estyn work "quite factual," focused on numbers, and argues qualitative work is needed to understand the story behind it and whether it connects to accountability-measure incentives, including anticipated effects of the shift to capped-9

Liz Williams: raises that schools are measured "only... on academic outcomes rather than the journey travelled by the child and the efforts put in... to nurture... well-being," particularly for vulnerable pupils — meaning there's currently limited incentive to retain challenging or lower-attaining pupils, something she says needs further scrutiny

Stone: cross-refers the committee to the Welsh Government's loneliness and isolation strategy, to which Samaritans made extensive representations; the strategy already contains a commitment to "use... approach to accountability to recognise inclusive schools and reduce incentives to remove pupils from schools" — Stone calls this "a really important commitment to make a reality," given what she frames as currently "perverse" incentives around the issue

Johnson adds a further open question: what happens differently to children who enter PRU/EOTAS provision earlier in their school career (years 7/8, 8/9) and loop back into mainstream, versus those who enter nearer the end of compulsory schooling and what becomes of them afterward — flagged as something the committee may pick up later in the session
**Support for pupils at risk of becoming EOTAS (Janet Finch-Saunders)**

Stone: this was a "major focus" of Samaritans' work, which concluded support currently "isn't" adequate, and that the issue is "not simply a question of the young person" but of the whole school environment's interaction with a young person's challenges; calls for a compassionate, confident, whole-school response to distress (which may not present as obvious distress, and connects to responding to disclosed suicidal thoughts); stresses that school may be a young person's "only safe place," a point many headteachers/teachers already grasp — citing inspiring restorative-justice approaches used by some Cardiff schools as a promising model, and noting strong educator interest in the report's findings since publication; frames the real opportunity as building on and generalizing existing good practice, given the severe, hard-to-reverse lifetime consequences (including elevated suicide risk) of not holding young people within education

Johnson: stresses the need to address both the individual and the "macro" picture — a statutory whole-school approach, echoing the committee's prior 'Mind over matter' work, so prevention operates across the entire school community from the earliest years through secondary school, keeping learner support "at the forefront" of how schools interpret pupil behaviour, tying back into ACEs awareness

recognize ACE impact; train teachers toward a confident, understanding response; learn from what already works; listen to young people's own voices (building on the committee's own prior direct-voice work); help young people build their own emotional literacy/self-awareness (citing international evidence on its value, developed alongside Wales's new curriculum health work); make health-and-well-being/mental-health content statutory within the new curriculum specifically to avoid entrenching inequality between schools with the "good will" to act and those that find it "harder" — summarized as "a menu," grounded in respecting and working with teachers' and schools' existing efforts and intentions

Johnson adds: identifying "the best support at this point in time" must be individualized, learner-voice-driven; flags an upcoming Mind Cymru "inclusive education inquiry" project specifically foregrounding young people's own voices in the evidence base, since current evidence is mostly data-driven or anecdotal; notes ongoing work still needed connecting PRU/EOTAS provision to the new curriculum

Liz Williams: raised in Samaritans' research-stage round table — participants were concerned about limited awareness/knowledge around additional learning needs, since these learners are both at elevated exclusion risk and over-represented among those excluded, especially "cusp" or undiagnosed cases (citing ADD/ADHD as common in the excluded cohort); diagnosis alone has limited value without proper understanding and support behind it — one participant estimated up to 50% of a classroom could have an additional learning need, meaning diagnosis without adequate support doesn't actually benefit the child; the deeper takeaway participants emphasized was the importance of genuinely inclusive schools giving every learner proper opportunity to progress, diagnosed or not

Johnson: can't speak to individual-school awareness specifically, but notes all-Wales work on the ACEs agenda is underway (citing his own former school, now trauma-informed and widening that work); flags a specific concern about EOTAS/PRU progress within the incoming curriculum, referencing education-minister comments (in response to Suzy Davies, January statement) about "disallowing" curriculum areas for individual learners — which he has no objection to in principle, but stresses the health-and-well-being learning area and mental-health/emotional-well-being content must stay "centre stage" for this especially vulnerable group, a matter he expects the committee to revisit during the forthcoming curriculum and assessment Bill

Stone: connects early trauma to loneliness/isolation's role in driving distress and suicidal ideation, citing research on "belongingness" as critical to human functioning; notes Samaritans is releasing forthcoming research specifically on middle-aged men whose early-years trajectories trace back to this dynamic, and connects higher exclusion rates among boys to disproportionately high suicide rates and related issues among men — urging the committee to see "this whole picture" and to recognize young people's own strength/resilience as an asset worth building on, framing this as a genuine opportunity for positive change (Finch-Saunders notes north Wales suicide figures specifically are "very worrying")

Liz Williams: previews the same forthcoming men's research as showing how often these men "fell through the net" repeatedly as children, with many missed intervention opportunities in cycles of inequality — reinforcing that early challenging behaviour is "the first signs of distress," making this fundamentally a preventative-agenda issue
Johnson: can't fully answer what's currently happening, citing the absence of a national data/information picture — part of why the push toward embedding this in the curriculum has grown

Bowden notes much of the panel's evidence is anecdotal (referrals, own research); Johnson confirms the planned Mind Cymru research targets exactly this evidence gap; notes rising self-harm concern generally, with a gendered pattern (an increasing focus on self-harm among girls aged 15-19 specifically); from his prior committee appearance (Time to Change Wales project) his experience is that outcomes depend heavily on a school's senior-management-team commitment — strong SMT leadership produces real progress, more "laissez-faire" SMTs produce less — reinforcing his case for statutory whole-school-approach guidance to avoid uneven outcomes

Bowden asks specifically whether progress in mainstream schools is following through into PRU/EOTAS settings; Johnson is candid he "couldn't give... an answer" right now, calling the inability to get a national feel for this "slightly concerning," while suspecting pockets of good regional/national practice exist that deserve wider visibility
**Off-rolling of pupils with mental-health problems (Dawn Bowden)**

Liz Williams: confirms this "certainly does happen," drawing on both Samaritans research and her own prior work in pupil referral units with vulnerable children; describes a pattern where children with undiagnosed learning/communication difficulties get labelled "naughty and disruptive," become anxious and unable to keep up, act out specifically to escape the classroom, and are consequently off-rolled rather than supported; cites a positive counter-example — a PRU where children became distressed and disruptive specifically on Friday afternoons, which staff correctly read (rather than dismissing as "ridiculous" disruption) as anticipatory distress about unsafe/unfed weekends at home, responding with compassion instead of discipline; stresses teachers "shouldn't have to do this alone" and need proper training/confidence, including to ask direct questions about self-harm or suicidal intent when warning signs appear (referencing Samaritans' "compassion in education" toolkit); concludes that without properly equipped/trained staff, off-rolling — especially at key stage 4, where it protects a school's attainment data — carries little disincentive as things stand

Bowden asks how prevalent the "naughty" labelling pattern is; Liz Williams: "absolutely" prevalent, driven by individual school/teacher experience — children (especially those with undiagnosed communication difficulties who otherwise seem "bright") get labelled naughty rather than understood as anxious or affected by unseen ACEs at home; notes children can also learn to "play up to" that label if acting out reliably gets them out of an anxiety-inducing classroom

Bowden observes that the "naughty" label itself becomes the barrier to getting proper support; Liz Williams agrees, noting formal diagnosis "opens... doors" to school support, and reiterates that embedding statutory emotional/mental-health content into school culture helps students themselves recognize when and how to seek help

Johnson: shares a Mind Cymru focus-group finding — a boy reluctant to disclose problems to a teacher who held both his pastoral and disciplinary roles, for fear of disbelief or being seen as making excuses for "poor behaviour" — a consideration he says shouldn't be over-generalized but matters from a learner's perspective; returns briefly to the off-rolling data (repeating the Estyn year-10/11 and steadier 1.5-2% figures, and the unexplained 500-600-per-year baseline), stressing the qualitative "why" remains unanswered, including how much relates to mental-health factors versus accountability-driven behavior at year 10/11 specifically

Johnson: hasn't specifically looked for evidence here, but notes Estyn's report found generally fewer off-rollings from Welsh-medium education into EOTAS — possibly reflecting a complete lack of local EOTAS provision in some Welsh-medium areas, or a different socio-economic profile (since exclusion correlates strongly with free-school-meal eligibility, and Welsh-medium schools' catchments can differ socio-economically); no specific work appears to have examined Welsh-medium EOTAS needs/provision; his unevidenced suspicion is that it's handled inconsistently, locally, likely more prevalent (by incidental local capacity) in west and north-west Wales

Stone: no specific research on this exact question, but frames delay through a broader lens: strong links exist between inequality and exclusion, with the most excludable young people also often carrying other disadvantages; any period out of education/support exacerbates pre-existing inequality and increases vulnerability through separation from a peer group, pushing young people to seek "alternative community"; cites a surge of interest since the report's publication from bodies worried about crime — Samaritans has engaged the youth justice board and police over "county lines" and home-growing drug operations exploiting exactly these disengaged young people; cites a recent Public Health Wales/Swansea University child-death review covering 33 youth suicide/suspected-suicide deaths, whose findings/recommendations noted these young people were "not... held" in education, training, or employment and had "slipped through" multiple systems, making the core message about not letting these gaps lengthen especially urgent

Liz Williams: no direct evidence on well-being impact specifically, but flags as a significant, related concern that there's no central data on how many young people are home-schooled — making this population potentially "hidden or invisible" and at heightened risk of exclusion-related harms; also flags uncertainty about how (or whether) unregistered children re-enter schooling if that's judged best for them; reiterates the "men's research" finding that home schooling might serve academic needs while leaving peer-group isolation and loneliness unaddressed, mirroring the later-life difficulty seen in men who lacked same-age peer interaction growing up

Johnson: distinguishes two related questions (delay before entering provision, and long-term effects of individual tuition) — individual tuition can be genuinely beneficial where a learner can't function in a group educational setting, but may be inappropriate longer-term, and is "very much an individual matter"; his main concern is the gap itself between leaving mainstream education and entering any EOTAS provision (due to capacity or other reasons) — while causation/exacerbation of mental-health issues within EOTAS isn't established, it "seems intuitive" that such a gap is unhelpful, both for education-rights reasons and for the emotional state of young people likely already in a "confused and troubled" place during that gap; references a 2016 Estyn report on EOTAS recommending CAMHS support within such settings, without knowing what progress (if any) has followed, and flags an open question about the overlap between mental-health and neurodevelopmental needs in this population

Stone: notes the loneliness-and-isolation strategy already commits to analyzing existing education and health data to explore correlations between EOTAS/exclusion and mental well-being (including loneliness/isolation specifically) — a "welcome" commitment, while stressing there may be both positive and negative effects still unknown, given how much remains unexamined overall
Gwenllian asks generally whether excluded young people get adequate support, not just educationally, and whether responsibility for coordinating it is clear

Johnson: suspects support happens locally in places but there's no national picture; notes the gap between exclusion and entering EOTAS provision (echoing earlier capacity-issue discussion) as itself evidence of what happens to these especially vulnerable children while "outside of the system"; on responsibility, states it formally rests with the local education authority, but stresses these children typically touch multiple institutions, so services must be "interwoven" around them; connects this to his planned "inclusive education" inquiry work, flags funding adequacy as a live concern, and suggests thinking of the system similarly to "corporate parenting" (with local-authority figures available on this, though he can't recall them offhand)

Liz Williams: adds that responsibility also partly sits with parents — but parents can only support a child (whether at exclusion risk or already in EOTAS) effectively if they themselves have adequate information about their child's educational rights and entitlements, which she notes likely varies by school/local authority

Johnson: stresses ensuring the new curriculum's EOTAS provision genuinely includes the whole-school approach, and that Welsh-medium availability is addressed nationally (possibly via local consortia), alongside how initial and ongoing teacher training (for both new and experienced teachers) will actually implement this — given that EOTAS learners tend to be especially vulnerable, prioritizing well-being alongside qualifications/certificates matters as a "vital point for the years to come"

asked specifically about professional-development recommendations, Liz Williams: reiterates the need to embed the inequality/challenging-behaviour link into training so it lessens exclusion risk, and specifically that mental-health training should be built into *initial* teacher training rather than remaining "supplementary," giving teachers both skill and confidence

Johnson: reiterates that statutory status for the whole-school approach ensures consistent knowledge/awareness/signposting throughout a school community, embedding mental-health/emotional-well-being "first," rather than "waiting for a problem," as "the key to improving the well-being of our future generations"

Stone: closes by hoping the wider community recognizes the inequality/ACEs link and the opportunity this represents to intervene before a young person falls "out of school, and out of anything, and out of sight"
chair thanks the panel, confirms a transcript will be sent for accuracy review
item 4 (papers to note): the Welsh Government's response to the committee's report on scrutiny of the 2020-21 draft budget; members note it without objection
item 5: chair proposes, under Standing Order 17.42, that the committee resolve to meet in private for the remainder of the meeting; members agree

exclusion-reason data (e.g. "persistent disruptive behaviour") is reductionist — the underlying causal story doesn't reach the statistical level, despite schools keeping detailed paper trails before any exclusion

non_verbatim_nodes.text: Prevalence is rising system-wide across Wales, straining school and PRU capacity alike.
What presents as difficult behaviour is often an unmet additional learning need; Swansea's referrals rose roughly fourfold in five to six years, and the system hasn't caught up.
Built with schools to give universal provision plus a staged escalation for learners needing more specialist help.
Most authorities are moving in the same direction, but there's a lag bringing everyone to a consistent standard.
Too early to confirm improvement, though Torfaen reports working toward it via a broader, more balanced curriculum.
Directors stress to schools and government that a learner's future progression matters more than hitting a fixed attainment level; Estyn has shifted its own messaging to match.
Brings health, social care, and education together, on the premise that in-school behaviour usually reflects a harder home situation.
Widespread staff training on adverse childhood experiences now gives teachers more context for behaviour than the profession had in the past.
Expected to add system pressure; England's parallel legislation saw ALN funding come under sustained tribunal pressure, to the point authorities nearly stopped contesting them.
Already high, with agreements to devolve as much money as possible to schools directly — not seen as a driver of exclusions.
Provision needs shift term to term and year to year, but funding is set once a year, so unplanned pupil moves create pressure with no spare budget to draw on.
When a child moves out of school into a PRU, the funding stays with the school until the next annual allocation, leaving a gap PRUs must absorb.
National and regional networks, conferences, and joint visits have improved practice-sharing between PRU and mainstream staff.
Money is "devolved," not merely delegated, to secondary schools against a monitored action plan, giving them resource to manage the process themselves.
A local authority handed PRU money to secondary schools under a partnership agreement so they couldn't keep moving learners between schools; it started well, though long-term outcomes are unknown.
Part-time timetables ease learners back into school, with support continuing (and only gradually reduced) after full return.
The most challenging, oldest learners are far harder to reintegrate into mainstream; focus shifts instead to further education and colleges.
A "second chance" move to a new school, with a cooling-off period and learner voice built in, since it doesn't always work out.
Safeguarding drives which providers are approved, balanced against not discouraging providers from coming forward at all.
Authorities can't quality-assure home tuition beyond what families choose to let them see, since access into the home is restricted.
Authorities use their own staff, not agency staff, for home or medical tuition, giving at least direct employment oversight.
Senior leaders are reviewing each school's alternative provision because arrangements that worked before are no longer fitting learner complexity or curriculum needs.

WLGA and ADEW worry that changes to EOTAS pupil registration could disrupt data, funding, and joint-working arrangements — specifically the funding-follows-the-learner principle and the shared ownership that stops schools quietly off-rolling GCSE-age pupils from their data.
Broad, balanced, inspected, and under local authority control — the panel is content here.
Quality assurance is far weaker once learners leave the PRU system; regional collaboration on the new curriculum is developing but not yet consistent.

ALN needs should follow learners into EOTAS, but support becomes increasingly hard to guarantee outside the tightly regulated PRU sector; Swansea wants a dedicated educational psychologist for its EOTAS learners but lacks the capacity.
Expertise is niche and slow to rebuild once experienced staff leave or retire; it's "more than just one person," it's a whole training package.

Newly qualified teachers currently can't work in EOTAS settings; the panel wants exposure built into initial teacher training and ongoing professional development, in both directions between PRU and mainstream staff.
Professional development for small EOTAS staff cohorts is still limited, though networks and conferences are helping.

Access to CAMHS varies across the three health boards in one region alone; a new designated education clinical lead officer (DECLO) role should strengthen partnership, alongside a universal well-being strategy including counselling, but current support "hasn't been great."
Wide rural regions like Powys (north to south) require long EOTAS travel distances even with provision in both halves of the county; more compact authorities such as Torfaen see far less of an issue.

Official exclusion statistics are reductionist (e.g. "persistent disruptive behaviour") and don't surface the underlying causes already documented in schools' own paper trails, which rarely reach a higher level of analysis.
Exclusions among younger children have risen substantially and are "very concerning," but the evidence is largely anecdotal and the reasons primary schools are excluding more aren't yet understood.
Around 4% of pupils are off-rolled, a sharp spike tied to end-of-key-stage-4 accountability measures.
A steadier 1.5-2% (roughly 500-600 pupils a cohort) are off-rolled every year, a normalised baseline whose causes need qualitative, not just quantitative, investigation.

Measuring schools on academic outcomes alone, not the journey or well-being effort invested in vulnerable pupils, discourages retaining challenging or low-attaining pupils; the loneliness and isolation strategy commits to rewarding inclusive schools and reducing the incentive to remove pupils.
Samaritans' report calls for confident, informed responses to distress from everyone in a school, since a young person's only safe place may be the school itself.
Include recognising ACEs, training teachers, learning from what works, listening to pupil voice, and building emotional-literacy skills, statutory in the new curriculum.

Diagnosis alone has little value without matching support in place, given up to half a classroom may carry some additional learning need; the deeper priority is an inclusive school regardless of diagnosis.

Trauma-informed practice is spreading (one governor's school became fully trauma-informed) but inconsistently across Wales; the new curriculum's health-and-well-being area is seen as the vehicle to embed emotional and mental well-being statutorily.

Samaritans' unpublished research on middle-aged men links childhood exclusion and peer-group isolation to elevated later-life suicide risk, tying belongingness to basic human functioning and framing early intervention as prevention.
Children with undiagnosed communication or learning needs get labelled "naughty," especially when they otherwise seem bright.
When the same staff member handles both pastoral care and discipline, pupils fear disclosure will be dismissed as an excuse for bad behaviour rather than taken seriously.

Estyn data shows fewer off-rollings from Welsh-medium schools, possibly reflecting socio-economic profile (free-school-meal eligibility correlates with exclusion) or a lack of Welsh-medium EOTAS provision itself — an area nobody has specifically studied, suspected to vary informally by local authority.

Time spent outside any education setting compounds existing inequality and vulnerability and heightens exposure to exploitation such as county-lines drug gangs, echoed in a Public Health Wales/Swansea University review of 33 youth suicides where young people had "slipped through" education, training, and employment systems entirely.

No central data exists on how many children are home-schooled, raising concern that some are "hidden" or invisible to services; academic tuition alone can address the curriculum but not the peer-isolation harms tied to the same men's research on later-life suicide risk.
Formal responsibility sits with the local education authority, but excluded children touch several institutions at once, so services need to be interwoven around them.
The panel suggests treating this vulnerable group the way corporate parenting treats looked-after children.
Parents can't advocate for their child's entitlements if they aren't given clear information about what provision the child is owed.
So every school has the same baseline of knowledge and ethos, not just those with a proactive senior leadership team.
embed mental-health training in initial teacher education
Rather than leaving it as optional supplementary training.
ensure the new curriculum covers EOTAS/PRU and Welsh-medium provision
Including how local consortia will implement it and how initial/newly-qualified/experienced teachers alike will be brought up to speed.

non_verbatim_nodes.text: McPherson (NDP) tables a Canadian Perinatal Mental Health Collaborative petition urging a national strategy with universal screening and funded treatment, citing 20% of women and 10% of men affected and an $11B annual economic cost.

Reid (CPC) asks the government to rescind Patented Medicine Prices Review Board changes and negotiate a national gene-modulator price, citing Trikafta's 90% effectiveness for cystic fibrosis sufferers.
May (GP) presents a pre-pandemic petition from her Sidney, B.C. riding citing nearly five million Canadians without a family doctor, worst in rural areas.

Vis (CPC) presents opposition to firearms confiscation, arguing enforcement dollars should instead target gangs and border smuggling and that "military-style assault rifle" is an undefined, political term; the chair reminds him petitions must stay a "prcis," not a speech.

Johns (NDP) tables a 1,198-signature Nova Scotia petition against open-net salmon farm expansion, citing risks to wild Atlantic salmon and existing lobster fisheries, and calling for a shift to closed-containment aquaculture.

Manly (GP) presents a petition calling for halting Coastal GasLink construction, RCMP exclusion-zone withdrawal, and honouring UNDRIP and TRC recommendations; he notes nation-to-nation talks had since begun.
Ratansi (Lib.) presents a Don Valley East petition asking that Canadian and foreign airlines be denied financial assistance until they fully refund COVID-cancelled flights.

Albas (CPC) presses Trudeau six times on reports that federal workers were told to ignore roughly 200,000 flagged-fraudulent applications; Trudeau never confirms or denies the memo, repeating that speed of help was the priority and fraud would be "cleaned up" retroactively.

Rayes (CPC) puts the same question to Revenue Minister Lebouthillier; she explicitly denies CRA told staff to ignore fraud, but cannot say whether a returning worker must repay the full $2,000 or only $500 per week worked, a gap Qualtrough later says "depends on individual circumstances."

Aboultaif (CPC) cites section 34 of the Statistics Act and asks whether a pre-market-open leak of economic data is a criminal offence; Bains calls the breach "completely unacceptable" and says it is "being looked into," but won't confirm an RCMP referral or commit that Liberal staff will cooperate, unlike the SNC-Lavalin precedent Aboultaif raises.

Ste-Marie (BQ) notes the large employer emergency financing facility bars illegal tax evasion but not legal use of tax havens by companies like the big banks; Trudeau says applications will be assessed case-by-case with a transparency requirement, without addressing the legality distinction directly.

Savard-Tremblay (BQ) cites a Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives finding that the 100 highest-paid CEOs earned 227 times the average worker in 2018, with 18% CEO pay growth even at loss-making firms, and demands an executive-compensation ceiling; Morneau confirms compensation conditions are coming, with facility funds barred from dividends or share buybacks and a tax-evasion screen.

Simard (BQ) contrasts a $1.7B orphan-well cleanup and a $500M EDC loan to TC Energy's Coastal GasLink pipeline (8.6Mt CO2/year) against the Prime Minister's green-recovery task force; Wilkinson defers climate questions to "beyond this phase of the crisis," with an interpretation outage forcing him to repeat the answer.

Simard notes the same $500M went to one pipeline project as EDC's entire 2017 softwood-lumber-tariff support for the whole forestry sector (58,000 Quebec jobs, $6B GDP); O'Regan cites the 2017 softwood action plan and strategic innovation fund rather than matching the liquidity figure.

Kwan (NDP) raises a single parent of four taxed on spousal/child support income but ineligible for CERB, unaddressed three weeks after the Employment Minister said she was "looking into it"; Trudeau acknowledges "gaps" from moving quickly but gives no fix timeline.

Kwan calls federal shelter funding "deficient," criticizes the 50%-chronic-homelessness-reduction target as too modest, and flags that Vancouver East's large urban-indigenous population received under 2% of pandemic urban-indigenous housing funds; Trudeau cites hundreds of millions already sent to shelters and defends the housing strategy as ambitious.

Kusie (CPC) calls the one-time up-to-$500 OAS/GIS payment, announced three months into the pandemic, evidence seniors are treated as an "afterthought"; Schulte cites an earlier ~$375-500 GST top-up as already delivered support.
Sgro (Lib.) and Blois (Lib.) thank Schulte for the day's announcement and press for continued advocacy; Schulte cites a $20M New Horizons for Seniors expansion for services like grocery delivery.

May (GP) flags well-run non-profit seniors homes with no revenue loss but rising wage and PPE costs and "nowhere to look for help"; Hajdu points to provincial health-transfer funding rather than a dedicated program.

Bergen (CPC) cites a constituent whose March 12 documents, including a doctor's note, sat unopened for two months; Hussen says he is not aware of a widespread issue but offers to investigate the individual case, citing redeployed front-line phone staff and pandemic-driven office closures.

Davies (NDP) notes over 80% of Canada's COVID deaths occurred in long-term care, the highest share among 14 comparable countries, with no province meeting minimum hands-on-care standards and for-profit homes seeing 2-3x the death rate of public/non-profit ones; Hajdu points to provincial/municipal jurisdiction while promising talks toward stronger national standards.

Davies links pandemic job losses to lost employer-tied drug coverage and asks for universal pharmacare "at the earliest opportunity"; Hajdu says a national pharmacare plan remains part of her mandate without a timeline.

Bergen (CPC) argues the Iver Johnson single-shot farm rifle, passed down generations, is being wrongly banned instead of targeting gangs and smugglers; Blair cites Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police and Ontario police-leader statements supporting a ban on weapons of military-combat design, and says the nine banned models share that origin, not hunting or sport use.

May (GP) asks the government to table the full legislative framework, including the buyback program, for first reading rather than delaying; Blair promises it "at the first opportunity," alongside other unspecified gun-control measures.

Dalton (CPC) describes a Maple Ridge firearms retailer stuck with unsellable banned-model inventory and eight employees at risk; Blair reiterates that weapons for lawful hunting and sport shooting remain unaffected.

May (GP) invokes Jonas Salk's unpatented polio vaccine and asks whether publicly funded COVID vaccine research will be shared globally, non-profit; Bains commits to an "open science," multi-jurisdiction collaborative model while still saying Canada will support its own IP where it drives the work.

May cites a Dalhousie Health Law Institute allegation that a Winnipeg-developed Ebola vaccine was delayed by a for-profit market-timing motive, and asks if the profit model itself will be examined; Bains highlights Canada's Ebola-vaccine and SARS-DNA-sequencing achievements without directly addressing the profit-motive critique.
